About

# About Zemanium.

Zemanium is a geothermal invention lab. We design the instruments, well hardware and models that hot wells need, test them in simulation against rules we fix beforehand, and publish what comes out.

01 / Facts

## The basics.

| Name | Zemanium (zeh-MAY-nee-um) |
|---|---|
| Founded | 2026 |
| Founder | [Toni Zemani](https://zemanium.com/about#toni-zemani) |
| Field | Enhanced and superhot geothermal: well integrity, flow control, sensing, power conversion and cost modelling |
| Stage | Simulation campaigns run on the first programmes; models, forecasts, records and drawings published; physical test campaigns next |
| Contact | [toni@zemanium.com](mailto:toni@zemanium.com) |
| Website | https://zemanium.com/ |

02 / Mission

## Make Earth's heat the world's power.

Our mission is to make geothermal the world's dominant energy source. Heat under our feet is available day and night in every country, and the obstacle is cost. We work on the equipment that decides that cost: wells that survive, flow that reaches the hot rock, instruments that keep working, and plants that convert more of the heat.

Our development target is firm geothermal power at $30 to $45 per megawatt-hour. The [cost guide](https://zemanium.com/guides/geothermal-electricity-cost) shows what a plant has to cost to get there.

03 / Method

## How we work.

1. Every invention goes through a simulated test campaign before any metal is cut. We write down the mechanism, the equations, the pass and fail rules and the conditions that would prove us wrong, and then we run it.
2. The rules that judge a simulation are the rules that will judge the bench test.
3. Every number carries a label: measured, vendor-stated, SIMULATED, assumption. A simulated result is never called a qualification.

05 / Founder

## Toni Zemani, founder.

Toni Zemani founded Zemanium in 2026 and leads its engineering and research. He writes the guides on this site and built the work behind them:

- the conduction model that matches the Nevada regulator's record of Fervo's Project Red well pair to 0.51 °F on nine steady months, with forecasts registered and time-stamped on 19 November 2026 and published as [forecast-audit](https://github.com/tonizemani2/forecast-audit) (doi:10.5281/zenodo.24396505);
- the replay of IDDP-1's production casing through the well's recorded history, which reproduces the 2014 video log in 88 of 128 sampled wells (SIMULATED);
- Pandora, a casing joint for superhot wells at 450 to 500 °C;
- the GEOPHIRES-based power-cost model and the [LCOE calculator](https://zemanium.com/lcoe-calculator).

Code and records are on GitHub at [github.com/tonizemani2](https://github.com/tonizemani2).

Thesis · [Toni Zemani](https://zemanium.com/about#toni-zemani) · 28 November 2026

# Energy After Singularity.

A thesis on the energy system after abundant research, with dated predictions. Solar with storage supplies about half of the world's electricity by 2045. Superhot geothermal, from rock at 400 to 450 °C, supplies the firm power: 1,650 GW in the full-win scenario, a fifth of the world's electricity.

Labels travel with the numbers: [MODEL] is computed from published correlations, SIMULATED is the result of a physics simulation campaign, vendor-stated is taken from the maker. Each of the 23 predictions names the public record that settles it.

## The thesis

In autumn 2026 Levent Alpöge and Claude completed a formal proof of the Generalized Riemann Hypothesis in six weeks, certified in Lean on 21 November. Two months earlier, 10,000 autonomous OpenAI agents had produced a Lean-checked blow-up construction for forced 3D Navier-Stokes. Research is becoming abundant.

This essay follows that trend to its end and describes the energy system that results. It assumes that digital research, design and multiphysics simulation run at near-zero marginal cost, and that embodied robots take the human field labour out of factories, mines and construction sites.

When research is abundant, energy is decided by what research cannot shortcut: physical tests, physical ageing, supply chains and conservation laws. Those constraints are known today, so the energy system that follows can be described today. Solar with storage supplies about half of the world's electricity. Superhot geothermal, meaning 400-450 °C rock reached by 8-12 km wells, becomes the leading source of clean firm power and of industrial heat up to 450 °C. Fission, fusion and orbital power each take a later and narrower place, and several well-funded ideas are ruled out by physics.

The centre of the argument is superhot rock. At 400-450 °C a kilogram of fluid carries four times the work it carries from today's 200 °C wells, so one pair of wells makes 40-55 MW where it now makes about 10. On good ground that power costs $25-$29/MWh. It runs through winter nights, burns no fuel and takes 1-3 km² of surface per gigawatt. Wells have already reached the depth, and every remaining step has a date in this essay.

![Figure 1: Superhot geothermal in six numbers. The 2045 figures are the full-win scenario ([MODEL]).](https://zemanium.com/assets/thesis/figure-1-key-numbers.png)

Figure 1: Superhot geothermal in six numbers. The 2045 figures are the full-win scenario (`[MODEL]`).

Firm power is power available in any hour of the year, including a windless winter night. This essay calls that hour the firm hour, and most of the argument concerns who supplies it.

The thesis rests on five claims:

1. Three things set the pace: how cheaply a technology can be tested, how long it waits in queues, and how much energy physical industry needs.
2. Solar with storage wins bulk energy and leaves the firm hour open.
3. Firm power has to be generated locally, and every surface source of it has a cost floor.
4. Superhot geothermal supplies the firm hour.
5. Earth has a heat ceiling, and growth past it moves to orbit.

At Zemanium we are building three of the links argued below: the superhot casing string (`U3`), downhole flow control (`U4`) and the reservoir scoring record (`U7`).

Part I describes the future these claims produce, with dates. Part II gives the method, Part III argues each claim through twelve propositions, and Part IV lists the 23 dated predictions that score the thesis.

## Part I: The future, stated in advance

Every date in this part is a prediction. A prediction number in brackets points to Part IV, which gives the falsifier and its probability.

### 2026-2031: grid queues

Demand for power grows faster than grids can connect it. Frontier training compute grows 4.6× a year while chip efficiency grows 1.21× a year (Epoch AI), so the power drawn by a single training run compounds at 3.8× a year. Global data-centre electricity grows from 485 TWh in 2025 to 900 TWh a year or more by 2030 (prediction 4).

A grid connection in the US or EU takes four to six years, and a Western reactor licence takes five to eight, so in these years buyers pay for speed. Hyperscalers run on gas engines installed behind the meter in 6-12 months, and clean firm contracts of 250 MW and more sign at $95/MWh or above to skip a three-year queue (prediction 21).

Geothermal enters at 200-240 °C. In the US West, 5-6 km granite wells are drilled in about twenty days (Fervo's Sawtooth 7 reached 5.93 km in 21 days in July 2026), and next-generation geothermal contracts are reported at $80/MWh or below by 2028 (prediction 5). Those contracts fund the superhot step. Superhot well hardware is engineered in simulation today, is proven on the bench in 2027-2029 and runs in field wells in 2028-2030. By 2030 a well producing from rock at 400 °C or hotter delivers electricity to a grid (prediction 7). Google's 50 MW contract with Quaise, signed on 17 November 2026, calls for superhot power as early as 2030.

In orbit, the first megawatt of solar-powered compute runs continuously by 2029 (prediction 3).

### 2029-2034: solar, chip efficiency and drilling depth

Robots take more than half of the field labour out of solar construction. Public sunbelt tenders clear unsubsidised solar with four or more hours of storage under $50/MWh by 2030 (prediction 10), and sunbelt solar with sodium-ion or iron-air storage falls below $35/MWh in 2028-2031. That leaves flat 200 °C geothermal in the US sunbelt a window of 2026-2030.

Chips get more efficient in the same years. Optical interconnects and 3D compute-in-memory cut the energy per unit of intelligence 30× to 100× by 2032-2034. If efficiency improves 30× while AI demand grows 50×, data-centre electricity plateaus near 900 TWh in 2031-2034. Firm power that was contracted at $65-$90/MWh on urgency alone is stranded in that plateau, while firm power below $40/MWh keeps selling.

Drilling reaches superhot depth. Granite wells of 8-12 km cost $15-$20 million in 2029-2032 (prediction 17), and operators sweep reservoirs at 400 °C and above in 2028-2031. Europe's rival is priced in the same period: Frankfurt's mix of wind, solar, eight-hour batteries and a 6% clean-fuel peaker reaches $53-$62/MWh in 2029-2034.

### 2032-2040: small reactors, orbital compute and fusion

Factory-built small reactors arrive in 2032-2038 with a cost floor of $52-$69/MWh. Orbital compute becomes economic in 2032-2036, once split-rail cooling cuts power and thermal mass by 24-30% and robotic fabs cut chip cost tenfold. Fusion delivers net facility electricity to a load after 2032 (prediction 9), and commercial D-³He fusion arrives in 2035-2040 at the earliest.

Geothermal is in commercial build-out by then. At least 50 GW of next-generation geothermal is operating or under construction worldwide by 2035 (prediction 12), and Lazard, NREL ATB or BNEF puts its unsubsidised low end at $45/MWh or below (prediction 11).

### 2045: the electricity mix

The world uses 65,000 TWh of electricity a year, supplied as follows.

![Figure 2: The 2045 electricity mix, with the energy each source supplies and the price it realises. Scenario shares, [MODEL].](https://zemanium.com/assets/thesis/figure-2-mix-2045.png)

Figure 2: The 2045 electricity mix, with the energy each source supplies and the price it realises. Scenario shares, `[MODEL]`.

| Source | Share of electricity | TWh per year | Realised price ($/MWh) | Its place |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Solar PV + storage | 50% | 32,500 | 20.4 | Daytime bulk and the open sunbelt; with thermal batteries, industrial heat above 500 °C |
| Superhot geothermal | 20% | 13,000 (1,650 GW firm) | 40.0 | The leading clean firm source: high-latitude winter grids, cold-craton metros, 100-450 °C industrial heat |
| Wind + clean-fuel peakers | 16% | 10,400 | 42.0 | Coastal corridors, limited by wake and permitting |
| Fission + hydro + early fusion | 14% | 9,100 | 48.0 | Hydro and fission, which generated about 7,200 TWh in 2024, plus state fleets (China), the coldest cratons, marine and defence |

Solar and geothermal sell different products. About 60% of solar's energy is midday sunbelt bulk that clears at $10-$16/MWh, while the firm hour clears near $40/MWh, so a firm source can hold a fifth of the system next to much cheaper solar.

The geothermal row is the full-win scenario (`[MODEL]`): 1,650 GW of firm capacity, which is 103× today's 16 GW fleet, plus 12,000 TWhₜₕ a year of 100-450 °C industrial and district heat from its own wells. Prediction 13 scores roughly the first quarter of it, the point where geothermal generates more electricity in a calendar year than nuclear fission, by 2045.

### After 2050: physical industry

Once intelligence is efficient, the load that keeps growing is physical: steel, hydrogen, aluminium, fresh water and chemicals. Global power scales 5× to 10× further, toward 50-100 TW in the 2050s and 100-500 TW beyond. At that scale geothermal is crustal heat mining, and each gigawatt takes 1-3 km² of surface pad where solar takes about 45 km².

### Past 500 TW: the heat ceiling

At 2,000 TW on Earth, 100× today's level, waste heat alone warms the planet as much as a doubling of CO₂. Growth past roughly 500 TW therefore moves into continuous orbital sunlight and radiates its heat to the 3 K sky. Launch from Earth carries the first 1-10 TW. Harnessing a millionth of the Sun's output is a 2060-2100+ project built from lunar and Mercurian material.

### Every call and its date

![Figure 3: Every YES call on one timeline. Appendix B lists each call, the NO calls and the predictions that score them.](https://zemanium.com/assets/thesis/figure-3-timeline.png)

Figure 3: Every YES call on one timeline. Appendix B lists each call, the NO calls and the predictions that score them.

## Part II: Method

### The premise and its limit

The Navier-Stokes result drew a specification dispute within weeks (`arXiv:2610.08144`), because the Lean formalization had proved a weaker statement than the natural-language claim. Even in pure mathematics, a formal compiler checks only the specification it is given. Abundant research can produce designs without limit, but each design still has to be tested in the physical world. Prediction 1 scores the premise itself.

With AI at full strength, every energy technology whose physics is not forbidden reaches its engineering limit. What remains is the schedule set by physical testing, supply-chain scaling and conservation laws.

### The four clocks

Progress after AGI runs on four clocks, and only the first is digital.

1. Clock 1 is digital design and simulation (Φ = ∞). It is compressed 5× to 20×, so years become weeks, and it already runs in casing design (Pandora, our superhot casing string), supercritical chemistry (`U6`) and AI plasma control.
2. Clock 2 is bench hardware and robotic factories (Φ ~ 10³-10⁵). It is compressed 2× to 4× for builders who run their own test rigs instead of waiting six months on a contract lab.
3. Clock 3 is physical ageing (treal), compressed 1× to 1.5×. Examples are 24 months of reservoir drawdown, 14.1 MeV neutron damage to a fusion wall and ten years of battery calendar ageing.
4. Clock 4 is liability, project finance and supply chains. It runs at 1× normally and 3× under a national-security emergency, and it covers $15M well-loss liability, the 24 months of operating history lenders want before debt, and the manufacture of 3,000-HP deep rigs and high-voltage transformers.

### The decision rule

Whatever physics permits and high-Φ hardware can iterate on gets solved on a Clock-2 schedule. Whatever violates a conservation law or an extensive floor fails cleanly.

Every YES and NO in this essay is that rule applied to one technology. We recompute vendor figures from first principles before using them.

### The eight forces

The rule is applied through eight forces, each argued in Part III.

| # | Force | Governing law | Argued in |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | Reality loop Φeff = Φ·T and geometric scaling G | Learning speed scales with how cheaply a small test stands in for the full system, times how faithfully the result transfers. The floor is fixed by extensive physics unless G shrinks mass per unit of output. | 1 |
| 2 | Permits, queues and time-to-gigawatt tGW | Grid queues take 4-6 yr, Western reactor licences 5-8 yr, behind-the-meter gas 6-12 months, geothermal pads in the US West 1-3 yr. | 2 |
| 3 | Robotics and the materials floor | Robots remove more than 50% of field labour. Hardware cost falls toward raw elements, smelting energy and capital. | 4 |
| 4 | Landauer vs. Gibbs | Energy per token can fall 30× to 100×. Steel, hydrogen, aluminium and desalination sit 1.5× to 3× above an irreducible ΔG. | 3 |
| 5 | Proof lowers the cost of capital | Cutting the cost of capital from 12% to 6% cuts annual capital charges by 41.5%. | 10 |
| 6 | Autarky, hardening and the two-planet split | China builds $30/MWh solar and storage, $65/MWh reactors and 11 km rigs. The UK rejected the $33B Xlinks cable. | 5 |
| 7 | Surface and subsurface density | Solar needs 45 km²/GW. Superhot geothermal needs a 1-3 km² pad and 22 km³ of granite over 30 years. Continental recharge is 9.6 TWₜₕ. | 4, 12 |
| 8 | Planetary heat ceiling | 2,000 TW of terrestrial waste heat adds 3.9 W/m², equal to a doubling of CO₂. | 12 |

### Labels on numbers

`[MODEL]` marks a figure computed from published correlations, `SIMULATED` marks the result of a physics simulation campaign, and `vendor-stated` marks a figure taken from the maker.

## Part III: The argument

### Claim 1. Three things set the pace: test size, queues and the energy needs of physical industry

#### Proposition 1. Abundant research speeds up only what can be tested small.

We tested 61 historical technologies in the Santa Fe Institute's Performance Curve Database. Mass-produced industrial hardware (cars, wind turbines, appliances) barely learned faster than site-built energy projects, at 4.0% a year against 3.2% (p = 0.21), while electronics learned at 46% a year. Replication alone does not bring cost down. What does is experimental variation across the design space, and it works inside two physical bounds.

The first bound is effective scale-factorizability:

Φeff = Cfull / Cproxy × Tproxy→full

Silicon learns fast because a $10 single-transistor test structure falsifies a $100M processor with transfer fidelity T ≈ 0.999, since Czochralski wafers are atomically homogeneous. Electrochemistry iterates in $100 coin cells (Φ ~ 10⁵), but pouch-scale swelling and ten-year calendar ageing do not show in a coin cell, so T ≈ 0.7.

Geothermal has both kinds of problem. Its component hardware (bits `U1`, casing joints `U3`, metal packers and chokes `U4`, alloy and brine chemistry `U6`) has high T: a $15k-$50k autoclave or frame test falsifies a $10M failure. Its macro-geology (500 m critically stressed faults `U9`, kilometre-scale fracture networks `U5`/`U7`) has low T, because a 5 cm rock core cannot contain an unmapped fault zone. The hardware therefore runs on Clock 2, and the reservoir needs field wells.

The second bound is geometric miniaturization G. Photovoltaics also has Φ ~ 10⁶, yet it learned at 12-17% a year where silicon learned at 46%, because transistors shrank and doubled output per kilogram every two years. Energy hardware meets extensive floors instead: 1,000 W/m² of sunlight, 300 Wh/kg of electrochemistry, √(αt) = 31 m of rock conduction. A high Φeff gets a technology to its physics floor sooner and leaves the floor where it is.

Predictions 2 and 22 score this proposition: a commercial service returns a third-party physical test record for a custom part in under seven days, and core-scale models predict field reservoir impedance.

#### Proposition 2. Until the queues clear, time-to-gigawatt outranks cost.

Per-run training power compounds at 3.8× a year, before algorithmic gains of about 3× a year, and capital and wafer supply cap single clusters around 2-5 GW in the near term. Against that growth, a 4-6 year interconnection queue or a 7-year reactor licence costs more than $150/MWh in lost compute lead during 2026-2031. Until the queues clear, a plant that can be built behind the meter quickly beats one that is cheaper on a spreadsheet.

Speed decides the order of arrival, and cost decides the final mix. Gas engines and combined cycles behind the meter cost $70-$85/MWh unabated and $80-$95 with carbon capture, face a four-year turbine backlog and depend on pipelines, which makes them the fast bridge of 2026-2031.

Predictions 21 and 4 score this.

#### Proposition 3. AI is the first load, and transforming atoms is the lasting one.

Today's AI silicon, at about 50 fJ per multiply-accumulate, sits 1.7 × 10⁷× above the Landauer limit (kB T ln 2 = 2.87 × 10⁻²¹ J/bit), and designers are using that headroom. In-die optical I/O (Marvell's $3.25B Celestial AI acquisition, closed February 2026; Lightmatter's 3D photonic Passage M1000) attacks the 75% of energy spent moving data. Together with 3D compute-in-memory and algorithmic compression, it brings joules per unit of intelligence down 30× to 100× by 2032-2034.

Transforming atoms has far less headroom. Steel takes at least 7.4 MJ/kg, hydrogen 33.3 kWh/kg, aluminium 6.3 kWh/kg and seawater desalination 0.8 kWh/m³. These are Gibbs free energies, and industry already runs within 1.5× to 3× of them.

Demand therefore has two regimes. AI drives the shock of 2026-2031, with a possible efficiency plateau in 2031-2034, and atomic industry, which needs baseload power and 100-450 °C heat, drives the growth to 100-500 TW. A firm source built for the first regime at $65-$90/MWh is stranded by the second. A firm source below $40/MWh serves both, selling into behind-the-meter AI demand now and powering metallurgy, chemicals, desalination and process heat afterwards.

Prediction 4 scores this, and the plateau is the item to watch after 2030.

### Claim 2. Solar with storage wins bulk energy and leaves the firm hour open

#### Proposition 4. Solar reaches the materials floor first, and its limits are latitude, land and long storage.

Commercial robotic field systems are already removing more than 50% of human field labour from utility solar and plant construction. Two examples are Terabase's autonomous *Terafab* ($130M Series C, March 2025) and Charge Robotics' portable solar factories. Hardware cost falls toward raw elements (silicon, iron, sodium, steel, concrete), smelting energy and capital. Firm solar with lithium-iron-phosphate or sodium-ion storage in the sunbelt costs $95 / $45 / $24 per MWh in the US and $60 / $33 / $21 globally in 2030 / 2035 / 2045. Solar wins daytime bulk everywhere, the open-land sunbelt below 40° N, and batch training loads.

Sunlight delivers 1,000 W/m², so firm solar takes about 45 km² per gigawatt, and above 42° N the winter resource collapses. The storage that would carry a dark week stays expensive: 100-hour iron-air sits at $107-$158/MWh of stored energy at 45% round-trip efficiency.

At 50° N the benchmark is therefore a mix of wind, solar, eight-hour batteries and a 6% clean-fuel peaker, at $90 / $58-$62 / $50 per MWh in 2030 / 2035 / 2045, or $55.5 if natural hydrogen fuels the peaker. The mix needs 75 km² per gigawatt, wind farms extract only 2-4 W/m² once wakes interact, and wind and HVDC take four to eight years to permit. A 240-hour-battery system would cost $144-$238/MWh, so the mix is the fair rival. It is also a generous one, because 15 ms of fibre round-trip spans 1,500 km, which puts North Sea wind, French nuclear and Spanish solar inside Frankfurt's latency cone.

The firm hour at high latitude and near dense cities is therefore still open at $50-$62/MWh, and that is the price Claims 3 and 4 have to beat.

Predictions 10 and 16 score this.

### Claim 3. Firm power has to be generated locally, and every surface source of it has a cost floor

#### Proposition 5. Firm power has to be generated domestically.

On paper, the cheapest firm power is desert sun moved north by cable. The UK rejected Xlinks' $33B, 3.6 GW Morocco cable in June 2025, at about $123/MWh, and even an overland 3,500 km UHVDC or superconducting link adds $32-$56/MWh and a sabotage risk. Intercontinental supergrids do not get built in the West.

Trade policy pushes the same way. Tariffs can raise US sunbelt firm solar and storage from $76 to $216/MWh today. Meanwhile China builds solar with storage at $25-$35/MWh, 63.9 GW of Hualong One reactors at $65-$80/MWh, the 125 MWe Linglong-1 small reactor (hot testing since October 2026) and 10.9 km ultra-deep land wells (Shenditake-1, 2025). Two industrial systems are forming, and each supplies its own firm power.

Tariffs do not protect expensive firm power for long, because domestic robotic construction brings US sunbelt solar and storage to $45-$55/MWh by 2030-2031 inside the tariff wall. Western firm power has to win on physics at $25-$41/MWh, and it gains a hardening premium when the plant sits 6-12 km under granite.

Not every load has to be supplied where it is used. Primary steel, aluminium, ammonia, hydrogen fuels and batch compute are tradeable: they can be made on firmed sunbelt solar at $21-$24/MWh and shipped by bulk carrier. On a first sizing they are 15-27% of the 65,000 TWh (`assumption`), and they belong to solar. The loads that cannot move are winter grids, electric heating, continuous inference, hardened sites and the local industry of cold and dense regions.

Those immobile loads are geothermal's market. Above 42° N and in dense land, their firm part is about 12,700-13,400 TWh a year (`assumption`), the same size as the 13,000 TWh of the full-win scenario. Hydro, fission and China's west-to-east lines hold about 6,500 of it, so 6,200-6,900 is open, and prediction 13 fits inside that open pool. The rest of the 13,000 comes from three places: the firmed wind mix of the same grids, which costs $50-$53/MWh against geothermal's $41; baseload on the best volcanic ground at $25-$29/MWh; and industry that stays onshore behind the trade walls described above.

#### Proposition 6. Each surface firm source has a cost floor above that range.

Appendix A has the full audit of every source. The floors are as follows.

- Large fission costs $185 / $160 / $140 per MWh in the US in 2030 / 2035 / 2045 and $65-$80 in China. With Φ ~ 1 every lesson costs a whole plant, and Western projects take 7-12 years against 5 in China. Fission holds China, Korea and France.
- Factory small reactors cost $145 / $78 / $52 per MWh. Robotics removes site civil labour, but the $22-$26/MWh of nuclear fuel, quality assurance, armed security and decommissioning does not compress. Small reactors win the coldest shields, defence bases and ships.
- Tokamak fusion costs $110 per MWh in 2035 and $55 in 2045. Its schedule runs on Clock 3, with 14.1 MeV neutron damage to the first wall, a lithium breeding blanket, 20 K magnets and a steam plant. It serves cold cratons and megacity cores after 2038.
- Pulsed fusion costs $65 per MWh in 2035 and $35 in 2045 if its physics clears. Helion's Polaris ran deuterium-tritium at 13 keV, where D-³He would return Pfus/Pbrem = 0.05, and at 60 keV with 1% carbon the margin is 2.06. D-D breeding still produces neutrons, and thirty years at 1 Hz is 9.5 × 10⁸ pulses. Pulsed fusion serves warehouse-scale point loads after 2035.
- Carbon thermal batteries own industrial heat from 500 to 1,600 °C. Antora's 5 GWh POET system has been live since May 2026 ($550M Series C, July 2026) and delivers heat at $37 / $24 / $18 per MWhₜₕ at 97% thermal round-trip efficiency. Turned back into electricity at 40-48%, the same energy costs $99 / $54 / $42 per MWhₑ.
- Natural hydrogen is still at the exploration stage at Koloma ($394M raised). Even at $0.75/kg at the wellhead and $1.50-$2.25/kg delivered, baseload power from a 58%-efficient hydrogen turbine costs $99-$138/MWh. White hydrogen wins steel, ammonia and peakers.

![Figure 4: Firm power cost by source in 2045, from Appendix A.](https://zemanium.com/assets/thesis/figure-4-firm-cost-2045.png)

Figure 4: Firm power cost by source in 2045, from Appendix A.

None of these reaches $25-$41/MWh as firm power in the 2030s. Prediction 9 scores the fusion call.

#### Proposition 7. Five further ideas are ruled out by physics.

The decision rule returns NO on each of the following.

| Idea | Call | The law it meets |
|---|---|---|
| Closed-loop conduction geothermal for bulk power (Eavor class) | **NO** on power, district heat only | Fourier conduction. Eavor's May 2026 Geretsried update reports 8.5 MWₜₕ from four flowing lateral pairs, with a nameplate of 1.3 MWₜₕ (about 0.17 MWₑ) per roughly 6 km pair at year five. That is 0.22 MWₜₕ/km, and 75-95 km of bore per 10 MWₑ over 30 years even at 400 °C (`[MODEL]`). |
| Pure mm-wave vaporisation to 10 km in wet granite (Quaise) | **NO**, stalls past 3-5 km | Energy and absorption. Vaporising rock takes 12-18 GJ/m³, which is 105-158 days at 0.3 dB/km attenuation, and less than 0.5 mm of water under 100 MPa of pore pressure absorbs 99% of a 100 GHz beam. Quaise's own Google contract (Project Obsidian) opens with conventional drilling into superhot rock, so superhot power is now contracted and its first phase drills mechanically. |
| Solar-firebrick topping on 200 °C wells | **NO** | Turbine moisture of 25.8%, and pure 600 °C solar firebrick with no wells beats the hybrid by $5-$11/MWh in every price regime (Figure 5A). |
| Desert LiBr absorption sub-cooling of a binary plant | **NO** | Second law. The LiBr loop exits at 75 °C or above (+0.50 MPa), yields no net gain on a 40 °C sink, and crystallises. |
| Hydrogen co-produced in a stimulated granite reservoir | **NO** | A 1.5 cm/yr reaction front, +30% hydration swelling that chokes 1 mm fractures in 6.5-82 days, and granite where the chemistry needs ultramafic rock. |

Predictions 14, 15 and 18 score these calls.

#### Proposition 8. Orbital compute arrives in the 2030s, limited by its radiator and by chip cost.

On 25 November 2026 the FCC granted SpaceX conditional authority (DA 26-1273) for up to one million Starmind satellites, in shells from 500 to 1,002 km at 30° and sun-synchronous inclinations, with the first satellite due by 2033. The AI1 satellite carries a 210 kW solar array, 175 kW average and 250 kW peak of Vera Rubin NVL72 compute, and a 160 m² double-sided liquid-ammonia radiator, at a `vendor-stated` 75 kW per tonne (13.3 kg/kW). Those numbers lead to five results.

1. The radiator runs at the memory limit. With emissivity ε = 0.90, fin efficiency ηfin = 0.80 and a 235 K Earth-facing sink at 550 km, it sits at 358.1 K (85.0 °C) at average load and 385.9 K (112.8 °C) at peak. HBM4 memory loses retention near 85 °C, so there is no margin at average load. A heat pump on the full load is 2.9% lighter than passive cooling with today's 5.0 kg/m² radiator, but 3.0% heavier with a 2.5 kg/m² radiator and 18.5% heavier with a 0.8 kg/m² film radiator. Split-rail cooling pumps only the roughly 15% of heat that comes from memory, from 345 K to 430 K, and lets the 85% from logic radiate passively at 390-410 K. That cuts power and thermal mass by 24-30% with the first two radiators and by 4.8% with film (Figure 5B).
2. The real mass is 19-24 kg per kilowatt. Compute, cold plates and regulators (about 1.0 t), 840 m² of array (about 1.2 t), radiator, pumps and shielding (about 1.0 t) and bus, propulsion and laser links (about 0.5 t) put AI1 at 3.5-4.2 tonnes for 175 kW. SpaceX's 75 kW per tonne, taken on the 250 kW peak, is 3.3 t, or 19 kg per average kilowatt. One million satellites deliver 175 GWₑ and take about 23,000-28,000 Starship flights.
3. The chips cost more than the power. At $30/kg to orbit, power and launch come to $43/MWh at 13-14 kg/kW. A 20% radiation and error-correction overhead on $30,000/kW processors adds the equivalent of $216/MWh. Satellites in 30° shells sit dark 35% of the time, and optical links of 100-400 Gbps against 7.2 Tbps of NVLink per processor rule out tightly coupled training. Orbit becomes economic in 2032-2036, once robotic fabs cut chip cost about tenfold, toward $3,000/kW.
4. The usable orbits are narrow. Packing multi-gigawatt arrays into dawn-dusk sun-synchronous ribbons to avoid eclipse raises debris collision flux more than 1,000×, and 700-1,002 km enters the inner Van Allen proton belt, where dose rises 10× to 100×.
5. A millionth of the Sun's output cannot be launched from Earth. 10⁻⁶ L☉ is 3.83 × 10⁸ TWₜₕ, 2,210× all the sunlight that reaches Earth. Physics permits collecting it, but that takes 2.81 × 10¹¹ km² of collector at 1 AU, 551× Earth's surface, or 84× Earth's surface at Mercury's 0.39 AU. Even as 0.5 kg/m² film the collector weighs 1.41 × 10¹⁴ t, which is 940 billion Starship flights and about 4.7 × 10¹⁵ t of propellant, roughly the mass of Earth's atmosphere. Launch from Earth caps near 1-10 TW.

Orbit is where the energy system continues once Earth's heat ceiling is reached. It takes asynchronous and batch compute from the mid-2030s and does not compete for the firm hour on the ground. Appendix C scales the constellation from one megawatt to a millionth of the Sun.

![Figure 5: First-principles physics audits. (A) Pure 600 °C solar firebrick beats the geothermal-firebrick hybrid in every price regime. (B) Split-rail orbital cooling cuts mass 24-30% where a full-load heat pump adds mass.](https://zemanium.com/assets/thesis/figure-5-firebrick-orbital.png)

Figure 5: First-principles physics audits. (A) Pure 600 °C solar firebrick beats the geothermal-firebrick hybrid in every price regime. (B) Split-rail orbital cooling cuts mass 24-30% where a full-load heat pump adds mass.

Predictions 3 and 20 score this.

### Claim 4. Superhot geothermal supplies the firm hour

#### Proposition 9. Geothermal loses at 200 °C and wins at 400-450 °C.

Across 51,882 onshore IHFC heat-flow measurements, 200 °C rock lies within 10 km under 65% of measured continental land, at a median depth of 8.5 km. Rock at 400 °C lies within 10 km under 7.5%. Its median depth is 18.5 km at constant conductivity k = 2.5 W/m/K, or 16.2 km with Vosteen-Schellschmidt granite conductivity k(T) falling to 1.8 W/m/K at 400 °C for heat production A = 1 μW/m³, and 19.0 km at A = 2 μW/m³.

The work available from a kilogram of fluid rises steeply with rock temperature. An exact IAPWS-95 isentropic ascent (hwh = hres − g z) gives a flow exergy of 172-176 kJ/kg from 200 °C rock and 617-756 kJ/kg from 400-450 °C rock at the 90th percentile of crust, about four times as much. Net output per well pair rises from about 10 MW to 40-55 MW at 150 kg/s through about 10 km² of swept fracture plane, and the hot column circulates by thermosiphon, so the plant needs no pumping after start-up.

At 200-240 °C the plant converts 12% of the heat to power and mines 137 km³ of granite per gigawatt over 30 years (at a 24% recovery factor; 60 km³ at 55%), against 22 km³ at 400-450 °C. Fervo's 3.0 design claims 15 MW gross per producer, about 11 MW net, but a static 0.137 km³ lateral box sustains 2.3 MWₑ for 30 years without wider sweep or make-up wells. As a result 200-240 °C geothermal costs $82 / $56 / $42 per MWh in 2030 / 2035 / 2045, and superhot costs $60 / $34 / $24-$41.

The cost falls in four steps, each with its own physical mechanism.

![Figure 6: (A) Work per kilogram of fluid and net output per well pair at 200 °C and at 400-450 °C. (B) Cost of geothermal power at each of the four steps, against the firmed wind mix at 50° N. [MODEL].](https://zemanium.com/assets/thesis/figure-6-ladder.png)

Figure 6: (A) Work per kilogram of fluid and net output per well pair at 200 °C and at 400-450 °C. (B) Cost of geothermal power at each of the four steps, against the firmed wind mix at 50° N. `[MODEL]`.

| Step (verified with IAPWS-95 / CoolProp) | Median crust ($/MWh) | 90th-percentile crust ($/MWh) | Mechanism |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1. Baseline 200-240 °C, today's rotary drilling | $106 | $82-$89 | Wells of 8.6 km / 4.3 km; 172-176 kJ/kg; 12% net efficiency. |
| 2. Adds trip-free monobore drilling (`U1`+`U2`), active flow control (`U4`), bankable capital (`U7`+`U8`) | $58-$65 | $42-$48 | Removes L²/(b·v) bit trips and L¹·⁷ steel. Thermal chokes stop q ∝ w³ thief zones across a 3-5.7 km² sweep. Insurance-backed capital falls from about 12% to 7.5% before tax. *(sCO₂ plume geothermal adds $324/MWh at 3% bought leak-off, or turns negative-cost under US 45Q credits of $85/t.)* |
| 3. Deep 300-400 °C factory superhot (9-10 km at the 90th percentile, 12-14 km at the median) | $40-$45 | $31-$35 | 371-617 kJ/kg; thermosiphon circulation; 25-42 MW per pair. Opened by `U3`, `U4` (which enables `U5`) and `U6`. |
| 4. Deep 400-450 °C superhot, $900/kW plant, $8/MWh O&M | $34-$38 | $25-$29 | 617-756 kJ/kg; 40-55 MW per pair at about 10 km² of swept plane; wells of 9-11 km at the 90th percentile and 16-18.5 km at the median. A bore of 0.25 m or more keeps wellhead velocity under API 14E erosion limits. Silica handling costs about $1.6/MWh. Delivers firm electricity and 100-450 °C industrial heat. The median-crust column needs wells deeper than `U2` and falls after 2045. |

Predictions 5 and 11 score this.

#### Proposition 10. Nothing in the superhot chain is forbidden by physics, and every link has a date.

Nine links separate today's wells from step 4. Each one is a problem in metallurgy, fluid mechanics, chemistry or mechanical drilling.

| Link | What must be true | Call and date | Evidence |
|---|---|---|---|
| `U1` Factory drilling, 5-6 km crystalline | Repeatable fast wells | **YES**, 2026-2028 | Already happening: Sawtooth 7, 5.93 km MD in 21 days, July 2026. |
| `U3` Superhot wellbore, ≥ 400 °C | Survive the thermal stress of a fully restrained string through quench cycling | **YES**, 2027-2029 | IDDP-1 parted on quench. Pandora, our casing joint and string, is engineered in simulation: 0/32 partings against 88/128 on the IDDP-1 replay (`SIMULATED`). |
| `U4` Zonal isolation and thermal flow control, 200 to 450 °C | A zero-elastomer packer holding ΔP ≥ 35 MPa and an active choke that stops q ∝ w³ thief zones | **YES**, 2027-2029 | Oilfield inflow-control devices already run at 200-280 °C. The device serves 200-250 °C wells first and scales to 450 °C. |
| `U6` Supercritical chemistry and silica | Carry 17-23 t/day of dissolved silica through the plant and back underground | **YES**, 2027-2029 | Dosing cost of +$0.07/MWh. |
| `U7`+`U8` Sweep longevity and the cost of capital | Prove ≤ 10% drawdown over 25 years and compress debt spreads 200-350 bp | **YES**, 2027-2029 | Already live as our `Project Red F1–F6` record: monthly scoring of Project Red (NDOM) and Cape Station GeoBlocks 1-3 (EIA-923). |
| `U5`+`U9` Superhot reservoir and aseismic licence | Hold about 10 km² of swept plane per pair at ≥ 400 °C with ΔV ≪ 10⁴ m³ | **YES**, 2028-2031 | Mazama (331 °C) and Krafla are testing sweep across the brittle-ductile transition. Eavor showed that zero seismicity opens €136M of EU/EIB capital. |
| `U2` Deep reach, 8-12 km granite | A well for ≤ $15-$20M | **YES**, 2029-2032 | No physics barrier: Kola SG-3 reached 12.26 km in 1989 and Shenditake-1 reached 10.91 km in 2025. Eavor is building a rig for more than 9 km. Trip-free wireline or coiled-tubing bit exchange and expandable monobore liners solve it mechanically. |

The hardware links (`U3`, `U4`, `U6`) are high Φ × T and run on Clock 2. An in-house 450 °C / 30 MPa wet-silica autoclave and thermal-cycle cell costs $50k-$120k and cuts one iteration from six months to seven days. Field proof follows in 2028-2030 in superhot test wells of the Mazama Athena, Krafla KMT-I and Japan class. Mazama Athena ($135M Series B) and Krafla KMT-I are drilling toward 400 °C now.

Sweep area sets the output per pair (`U5`+`U7`). Conduction into a fracture plane fixes how much flow each square kilometre can heat for 30 years. At 150 kg/s, 5.7 km² of plane loses 34% of the injection-to-reservoir temperature difference by year 30 (112 K), while about 10 km² holds the loss under 10%. At that limit 3-5.7 km² carries 46-87 kg/s, which is 12-32 MW of the 40-55 (single-plane Bodvarsson-Gringarten solution, `[MODEL]`). Output per pair is therefore a stimulation specification, and the cost tolerates a miss. With two $17.5M wells, $900/kW of plant and $8/MWh of O&M, a pair delivers $25.6/MWh at 47.5 MW, $29 at 32 MW and $34 at 23 MW. It stays under the $47 that beats Frankfurt's $53 rival after seismic drag all the way down to 13 MW per pair.

The remaining link is finance, on Clock 4. Cutting the pre-tax cost of capital from 12% to 6% cuts annual capital charges by 41.5% and the cost of energy by 25-37%. At a 4.3% Treasury yield, senior project debt at +225 bp (6.55%) at a 75% debt share with 11% equity gives about 7.7% before tax. Infrastructure debt normally waits 24 months for operating history. A live, scored longevity record with AA-backed parametric insurance compresses the spread by 200-350 bp without waiting five years per basin.

Predictions 6, 7, 8, 17 and 19 score this proposition.

#### Proposition 11. With those links in place, superhot geothermal wins the firm hour where solar cannot.

A 25,000-draw Monte Carlo (`[MODEL]`) runs superhot geothermal against its rivals in six markets, five of which appear in Figure 7. It includes explicit silica heat-exchanger costs, +$6/MWh of European seismic drag, the $53-$62/MWh Frankfurt mix, $52-$69/MWh factory small reactors and $24-$31/MWh sunbelt solar with storage.

Geothermal that stays at 200 °C loses everywhere by 2045, with a win rate of 0-11%. With `U2` and `U3` to `U6` delivered, geothermal is the leading clean firm source in 2045 across high-latitude Europe (88% win rate at $41/MWh) and in cold-craton metros such as Northern Virginia and Chicago (60% at $47/MWh, against $53 for wind with peakers and $61 for nuclear). It is co-winner in the best ground of the Western US at $32/MWh (35%). In the sunbelt the model picks solar, as Claim 2 says: geothermal wins 18% of draws in the tariffed US sunbelt and 1% in the untariffed global sunbelt.

![Figure 7: Probability that geothermal is the leading clean firm source, by market and year, on the YES schedule of Part I (U3 to U6 2027-2029, U2 2029-2032). [MODEL].](https://zemanium.com/assets/thesis/figure-7-win-probability.png)

Figure 7: Probability that geothermal is the leading clean firm source, by market and year, on the YES schedule of Part I (`U3` to `U6` 2027-2029, `U2` 2029-2032). `[MODEL]`.

The markets it wins impose two conditions. Northern Virginia, Chicago and London sit on cold basins, with 200 °C at 8-10 km and 400 °C at 16-20 km, so wells of 12-14 km meet rock at 240-350 °C there. Where that rock reaches 300 °C, which the warmer half of the range does by 14 km, a pair delivers 20-30 MW at $35-$43/MWh with $20-$25M wells, and $45-$53 if the plant costs twice the $900/kW of the superhot case (`[MODEL]`). The rivals there are wind with peakers at $53 and nuclear at $61. The 12 km wells are `U2`, the 14 km wells are prediction 23, and the 400 °C case in those basins follows after 2045 at 16-20 km. Frankfurt and Zurich sit inside Europe's strictest seismic-moratorium belt, where Basel (ML 3.4), St. Gallen (ML 3.5) and Strasbourg (ML 3.6) all forced shutdowns. In that belt superhot plants run aseismic, pressure-balanced circulation (`U4`+`U7`+`U9`) and publish their pressure-balance and seismicity records.

The 1,650 GW of the full-win scenario is about 70,000 deep wells. That takes some 500 rigs drilling flat out for thirteen years, or about 2,000 in the last year of a ramp of 42% a year, which is the US shale fleet at its peak rebuilt for depth (`[MODEL]`). The 12,000 TWhₜₕ of heat takes its own wells on top: about 19,000 if superhot doublets supply it as steady process heat, and two to four times that from cooler rock or for seasonal district heat (`[MODEL]`). About 150-200 land rigs worldwide reach 8-12 km today, and custom 100 MW steam turbines carry four-year backlogs, so the build uses standard machinable alloys, automated electric rigs and factory-built 10-20 MW power skids. The ramp starts from the 1.4 GW under contract in late 2026, and 50 GW by 2035 is 5.2 doublings from there.

Predictions 12 and 13 score this.

### Claim 5. Earth has a heat ceiling, and growth past it moves to orbit

#### Proposition 12. Past 10 TW geothermal is heat mining, and past about 500 TW waste heat limits power on Earth.

Natural continental heat flux is 9.6 TWₜₕ, about 2.4 TWₑ, so scaling geothermal past 10 TW means mining stored heat. The global stock lasts more than 1,000 years, and a local block lasts 25-30 years. The advantage is land: a 1-3 km² pad per gigawatt against about 45 km² for solar, which leaves urban and agricultural land alone while supplying the 100-450 °C heat and baseload that atomic industry runs on (Proposition 3).

Waste heat sets the upper bound. At 2,000 TW on Earth, 100× today's level, direct waste heat adds 3.9 W/m², equal to a doubling of CO₂. Growth past roughly 500 TW moves to continuous orbital solar that radiates to the 3 K deep-space sink, with the mass and radiator limits of Proposition 8.

## Part IV: The scored predictions

Each prediction below names a public record that settles it yes or no by a date, and carries the probability we assign. Predictions 1-13 were registered on 26 November 2026. Predictions 14*-22* were added on 27 November 2026, after the physics audit, and prediction 23* on 28 November 2026. All are scored by Brier score.

| 23* | A well reaches ≥ 14.0 km TVD in crystalline basement | 2045 | 0.55 | The record is 12.26 km (Kola SG-3, 1989). A steel string tapered about 4 to 1 in cross-section hangs 14 km at 75% of V-150 yield (`[MODEL]`), so the limit is borehole stability and budget. Opens the cold basins beyond `U2`. |

## Conclusion

The energy system after research waits on tests, wells, rigs and years, and each of those can be counted. The count gives sunlight the bulk of the world's energy wherever land is open and the sun is high. It gives the firm hour, the winter grid and industrial heat up to 450 °C to rock at 400-450 °C, reached by wells of a depth that has already been drilled, through nine links that each have a mechanism and a date. By 2045 that is 1,650 GW of firm power, 103× today's fleet and a fifth of the world's electricity. Fission, fusion and orbital power arrive where their own physics places them, and growth moves to orbit once the planet's heat budget is full. The first prediction resolves in 2027.

| Fusion A: high-field D-T tokamak (CFS) | n/a / $110 / $55 | Φ ~ 1-10. 3-6 yr (NRC Part 30 + tritium handling) | 14.1 MeV first-wall damage, lithium breeding blanket, 20 K HTS magnets, steam plant. 1.2 km²/GW | Cold cratons and megacity cores after 2038 |
| Fusion B: pulsed FRC (Helion) | n/a / $65 / $35 (post-2034) | Φ ~ 10³. 1-2 yr (NRC Part 30, proposed Feb 2026) | Polaris ran D-T at 13 keV (fusion-to-bremsstrahlung power 0.05 for D-³He); 2.06 at 60 keV (1% C); D-D breeding is not aneutronic; 9.5 × 10⁸ pulses per 30 yr. 0.4 km²/GW | Warehouse point loads after 2035, if bremsstrahlung and > 90% energy recovery clear |
| Orbital compute (Starmind AI1) | Equivalent $90 / $42 / $22 power; +$216/MWh chip overhead at $30k/kW | Φ ~ 10⁴. 1-2 yr (FCC DA 26-1273: 1M satellites, first by 2033) | 175 kW average on a 160 m² radiator (85 °C at fin efficiency 0.8, zero HBM4 margin); real mass ~19-24 kg/kW; 35% eclipse in 30° LEO; optical link far below NVLink. 0 km² on Earth; vacuum LEO | Asynchronous and batch compute after 2033, once robotic fabs cut chip cost ~10×; growth past 500 TW |
| Geothermal A: 200-240 °C EGS (Fervo 3.0 class) | $82 / $56 / $42 | Hardware Φ ~ 10⁴; reservoir T ≪ 1. 1-2 yr US federal West; 4-7 yr EU seismic | 12% net efficiency; a 0.137 km³ box sustains 2.3 MWₑ for 30 yr without wider sweep or make-up wells; thief zones (flow scales with aperture cubed). 3.5 km² pad; 137 km³ granite/GW | US West clean firm PPAs in 2026-2031, the commercial bridge that funds superhot |
| Geothermal B: deep 400-450 °C superhot (`U2` + `U3` to `U6`) | $60 / $34 / $24-$41 | Hardware Φ ~ 10⁴; reservoir T ≪ 1. 2-4 yr (aseismic balanced circulation) | Solved by Pandora (`U3`), thermal chokes (`U4`, enabling `U5`), silica chemistry (`U6`), and 8-12 km monobore (`U2`). 1.1-3 km² pad; 22 km³ granite/GW | The leading clean firm source on Earth: high-latitude winter grids, cold-craton metros, 100-450 °C industrial heat, sovereign bunkers |

## What Zemanium builds.

We are building three of the links in this thesis. [Pandora](https://zemanium.com/#pandora) is the casing joint and string for wells at 450 to 500 °C (`U3`). Downhole flow control (`U4`) is on the [research page](https://zemanium.com/room/). The reservoir scoring record (`U7`) is live as the [Project Red tracker](https://zemanium.com/fervo-project-red), where a registered forecast is scored against the Nevada regulator every month.

The [superhot rock guide](https://zemanium.com/guides/superhot-rock-geothermal) covers what wells above 375 °C have measured so far, and the [papers](https://zemanium.com/papers/) cover the casing record and the design rules for the quench.

If you operate, design or finance hot wells, or you want to argue with a prediction, write to [toni@zemanium.com](mailto:toni@zemanium.com).

## Common questions.

### What is the future of geothermal energy?

In this thesis superhot geothermal becomes the leading source of clean firm power. The full-win scenario is 1,650 GW by 2045, a fifth of the world's electricity and 103 times today's 16 GW fleet (model scenario). The step that gets it there is hotter rock: 400 to 450 °C, reached by wells of 8 to 12 km.

### What is superhot geothermal?

Geothermal power from rock at 400 to 450 °C. A kilogram of fluid from that rock carries about four times the work it carries from today's 200 °C wells, so one pair of wells makes 40 to 55 MW where it now makes about 10.

### Will geothermal be cheaper than solar?

Solar with storage stays the cheapest bulk energy and supplies about half of the world's electricity in 2045, at a realised $20.4 per MWh. Superhot geothermal sells firm power, available in any hour of the year, at $25 to $29 per MWh on good ground and a realised $40 per MWh across the 2045 fleet.

### Geothermal or nuclear for firm power?

The thesis puts factory-built small reactors at $52 per MWh in 2045 and large fission in the United States at $140, against $24 to $41 for superhot geothermal. Prediction 13 gives a probability of 0.60 that geothermal generates more electricity than nuclear fission in a calendar year by 2045.

### How are the predictions scored?

Each of the 23 predictions names a public record that settles it yes or no by a date, and carries a probability. All are scored by Brier score. Predictions 1 to 13 were registered on 26 November 2026, 14 to 22 on 27 November and 23 on 28 November. The first resolves in 2027.

Tracker · Toni Zemani · updated 24 November 2026

# Fervo Project Red: the monthly record against our registered forecast.

Project Red, Fervo Energy's pilot well pair in Nevada, produced 316 °F at the wellhead in July 2026, down from a 347 °F plateau in 2024, according to the Nevada regulator's monthly record. We registered a forecast for every month to December 2027 and score it here as each new month is published.

Monthly values are measured and operator-reported to the Nevada Division of Minerals, copied without changes. The forecast is [MODEL], frozen and time-stamped on 19 November 2026. Independent analysis from public records; not investment advice. Zemanium holds no position in any security.

01 / Record

## What the regulator's record shows.

The producing well delivered 343 to 347 °F through most of 2024 and 2025. From December 2025 the monthly mean fell every month: 342, 341, 338, 336, 334 and 332 °F in May 2026. June read 242 °F in a month with 32% less production, and July read 316 °F.

![Line chart of Project Red's monthly wellhead temperature from December 2023 to July 2026, followed by the shaded forecast band to December 2027](https://zemanium.com/assets/charts/project-red-record.svg)

Chart free to reuse under CC BY 4.0 with credit to Zemanium. Months under 1 million gallons or below 230 °F are left off the line and kept in the table and data file.

| Month | Wellhead temperature | Produced, million gallons | Injection temperature |
|---|---|---|---|
| Aug 2025 | 345 °F | 19.8 | 174 °F |
| Sep 2025 | 115 °F | 6.4 | 58 °F |
| Oct 2025 | 320 °F | 20.6 | 171 °F |
| Nov 2025 | 344 °F | 24.4 | 170 °F |
| Dec 2025 | 342 °F | 25.6 | 171 °F |
| Jan 2026 | 341 °F | 25.7 | 171 °F |
| Feb 2026 | 338 °F | 24.0 | 172 °F |
| Mar 2026 | 336 °F | 25.8 | 168 °F |
| Apr 2026 | 334 °F | 25.0 | 86 °F |
| May 2026 | 332 °F | 26.7 | 92 °F |
| Jun 2026 | 242 °F | 18.2 | 75 °F |
| Jul 2026 | 316 °F | 22.8 | 86 °F |

The temperature of the water sent back down changed in April 2026, from about 170 °F to between 75 and 92 °F. Colder injection cools the fractures faster, so our forecast uses the cold-reinjection case from that month on.

02 / Forecast

## What we forecast, and when it was fixed.

We fitted a conduction model of the fractured rock to nine steady months. It matches them with a root-mean-square error of 0.51 °F. Twenty-one model runs of 1,440 met that fit, and their spread sets the band. The forecast files were hashed and time-stamped by two independent authorities on 19 November 2026, before any of the forecast months were published.

- December 2026: median 318.1 °F, band 312.0 to 324.6 °F.
- July 2027: median 298.0 °F, band 286.9 to 310.6 °F.
- December 2027: median 284.6 °F, band 265.8 to 300.0 °F.

The model also says how much of the stated fracture area exchanges heat: 32% to 63% across the accepted runs. That figure decides how long a well pair of this design stays hot.

03 / Score

## Score so far.

Each month is scored on the 7th after the regulator publishes it. The latest workbook, dated 29 September 2026, runs to July 2026, so the first forecast month is still to come.

| Month | Forecast median | Band | Regulator value |
|---|---|---|---|
| Aug 2026 | 328.1 °F | 324.2 to 332.6 °F | next regulator workbook |
| Sep 2026 | 325.5 °F | 321.2 to 330.5 °F | next regulator workbook |
| Oct 2026 | 323.0 °F | 318.2 to 328.5 °F | next regulator workbook |
| Nov 2026 | 320.6 °F | 315.2 to 326.6 °F | next regulator workbook |
| Dec 2026 | 318.1 °F | 312.0 to 324.6 °F | next regulator workbook |

04 / Water

## How much water comes back.

Over 18 steady months, 72.7% of the injected volume came back up the producer, or 65.9% by mass. The ratio has not moved in 2.3 years: +0.2 points a year, plus or minus 1.5. Since December 2023 the pair took in 192.9 million gallons more than it returned.

05 / Questions

## Common questions.

### What is Fervo Project Red?

Project Red is Fervo Energy's first enhanced geothermal well pair, drilled at Blue Mountain in Humboldt County, Nevada. Its monthly production and injection are reported to the Nevada Division of Minerals under permits 1505 and 1506, which makes it the only enhanced geothermal production history in the public record.

### Is Project Red cooling down?

Yes, on the regulator's monthly wellhead metric. The record held 344 to 347 °F in steady months from May 2024 to November 2025 and read 332 °F in May 2026 and 316 °F in July 2026.

### Why is Fervo stock down?

Fervo Energy listed on Nasdaq as FRVO on 13 May 2026 after pricing its offering at $27 a share. A short seller report published in 2026 cited Project Red's temperature and water record. We checked 33 public claims about the well pair, from the short seller, the company and others, against the regulator's data; the audit is public and each verdict follows a written rule.

### What does Project Red mean for Cape Station?

Cape Station in Utah uses a later well design at larger scale and reached first power on 24 September 2026, by the company's account. Project Red is the only well pair with a public monthly record, so it is the best public evidence for how fast this kind of reservoir cools. Our forecast F5 covers a Cape-class producer.

### When is the next update?

On the 7th of each month after the Nevada Division of Minerals publishes a new workbook. Each update adds the new months to the chart and scores them against the registered band.

06 / Data

- MCP server for AI agents: `https://zemanium.com/mcp`. Tools return the record, the forecast, Nevada plant output and geothermal cost cases.

Guide · [Toni Zemani](https://zemanium.com/about#toni-zemani) · 28 November 2026

# Closed-loop geothermal: how sealed wells make power and heat.

A closed-loop geothermal system circulates a fluid through sealed pipe or wellbore in hot rock and takes the heat by conduction, so no water is drawn from the ground and no rock is fractured. The name covers two very different machines: deep loops kilometres down that make electricity and district heat, and shallow loops beside a building that feed a geothermal heat pump. Eavor's first deep loop at Geretsried, Germany, produced about 8.5 MW of heat in 2026, as the company predicted before drilling.

Geretsried figures are company statements by Eavor Technologies. Cost figures are from a 2023 study by the National Laboratory of the Rockies (NLR, formerly NREL) and Sandia National Laboratories. Heat pump figures are from the US Department of Energy. Depth and work-per-kilogram figures are Zemanium model results, labelled [MODEL].

01 / Mechanism

## How does a closed-loop geothermal system work?

![Diagram of three closed-loop geothermal designs: a deep U-loop with two wells joined by sealed laterals, a coaxial single well with an insulated inner pipe, and a ground-source heat pump with shallow vertical loops beside a house](https://zemanium.com/assets/charts/closed-loop-geothermal-diagram.svg)

Three closed-loop designs. In each, the fluid stays inside the pipe or wellbore and heat reaches it by conduction through the rock. Not to scale. Free to reuse under CC BY 4.0 with credit to Zemanium.

1. A pump, or in a deep loop the difference in density between cold and hot fluid, drives the fluid down the inlet.
2. The fluid runs through sealed wellbore or pipe in contact with warm rock, and heat conducts into it.
3. The warmed fluid returns to the surface.
4. At the surface it drives a power plant, usually an organic Rankine cycle, or a heat exchanger for district heating, or a heat pump in a building.
5. The cooled fluid goes back down the same loop. It never mixes with groundwater.

Because heat arrives only by conduction, the output of a deep loop scales with the area of wellbore in contact with hot rock and with the temperature of that rock. That is why deep closed-loop designs drill long horizontal laterals, and why they gain so much from depth.

02 / Designs

## What are the types of closed-loop geothermal systems?

| Design | Layout | Use | Example |
|---|---|---|---|
| Multilateral U-loop | two vertical wells joined by many horizontal laterals | power and district heat | Eavor-Loop at Geretsried, Germany, first power to the grid December 2025 |
| Coaxial | one well with an insulated inner pipe: fluid flows down the outer annulus and up the centre | heat, small power | modelled for thousands of designs in NLR and Sandia's 2023 closed-loop database |
| Conductive-material system | wellbore surrounded by thermally conductive material that draws heat from a wider volume of rock | power | XGS Energy: 150 MW agreement with Meta in New Mexico, announced June 2025 |
| Ground-source heat pump loop | horizontal, vertical or pond loops of plastic pipe near a building | heating and cooling buildings | by the Department of Energy's guide, the most common way to heat and cool with geothermal |

The companies behind each approach are in our [guide to geothermal companies](https://zemanium.com/guides/geothermal-companies).

03 / Record

## What Eavor's Geretsried loop produced.

Geretsried, in Bavaria, is the first commercial-scale closed-loop geothermal project. It sits on the site of an earlier conventional project whose wells found rock that was hot but dry. Eavor's technical update of 2026 gives these results, all company statements:

- Design: four loops of 12 lateral pairs each, for a nameplate of 8.2 MW of electricity or 64 MW of heat.
- Loop 1: six lateral pairs drilled and intersected at a measured depth of about 8,000 m, with four contributing to flow.
- Heat: about 8.5 MW, the output predicted for four pairs before drilling. Each pair produces more than 2 MW of heat now and is expected to settle at 1.3 MW after five years, the basis of the nameplate.
- Power: the Turboden organic Rankine cycle plant converts about 4.3% of the heat to electricity at the 11.8 MW average heat duty since start-up, because it is sized for the full four-loop project.
- Fluid loss: 0.5% to 2% of the circulating fluid, after sealing the laterals with Eavor's Rock-Pipe; about 0.1% expected in deeper basement rock.
- Lesson: cement behind the casing let fluid pass between the two drilling rigs, which forced one rig to work at a time and doubled drilling time and cost. Eavor has changed its cementing design for future loops and expects each new lateral pair to take about three weeks.

Eavor states that loops built this way are cost-competitive for European district heating in an average gradient of 30 °C per km, and that drilling deeper gives a path to electricity below $75 per MWh: in that gradient, it puts the output of a 15 km loop at 20 MW of electricity, against 2 MW at Geretsried.

04 / Cost

## How much does closed-loop geothermal cost?

For heat, little; for electricity, it depends on how hot the rock is. NLR and Sandia ran millions of simulations for their 2023 closed-loop database. Their worked example is one U-loop:

| Input or result | Value |
|---|---|
| Vertical depth | 3,000 m |
| Horizontal lateral | 9,000 m |
| Rock gradient and bottom temperature | 60 °C per km, 205 °C |
| Water flow | 20 kg/s |
| Average heat output | 3.9 MW |
| Average electricity output | 285 kW |
| Drilling cost, at $1,000 per metre | $15 million |
| Levelized cost of heat | $31 per MWh |
| Levelized cost of electricity | $438 per MWh |

The same loop sells heat at a district-heating price and electricity at several times the $67 to $111 per MWh of a new conventional geothermal plant in Lazard's 2026 estimate, shown in our [cost guide](https://zemanium.com/guides/geothermal-electricity-cost). Electricity from a loop gets cheaper with hotter rock, more laterals per well and cheaper drilling per metre. Our [LCOE calculator](https://zemanium.com/lcoe-calculator) shows how each input moves the price.

05 / Depth

## Why closed loops need depth.

A loop collects heat only through its walls, so hotter rock pays twice: more heat flows in, and each kilogram of hot fluid carries more work. At 200 °C a kilogram can deliver 172 kJ of work at the wellhead; at 300 °C, 354 kJ. Across the world's measured continental land, rock reaches 200 °C at a median depth of about 8.5 km.

[MODEL] · IAPWS water properties and IHFC Global Heat Flow Database 2024 · 27 November 2026

Where that heat lies shallow is on our [geothermal map](https://zemanium.com/guides/geothermal-map), and how fast rock heats with depth is in our [geothermal gradient guide](https://zemanium.com/guides/geothermal-gradient).

06 / Heat pumps

## Closed-loop geothermal heat pump systems.

Most people who search for a closed-loop geothermal system want to heat or cool a house. The US Department of Energy describes four ground-loop types; three are closed loops:

- Horizontal: usually the most cost-effective for homes, especially new construction with enough land. It needs trenches at least four feet deep.
- Vertical: used where land is limited or the soil is too shallow for trenches, with holes drilled into the bedrock. It can cost more but uses less land and disturbs less of the site. The holes run 100 to 400 feet deep, as our [wells guide](https://zemanium.com/guides/geothermal-wells#heat-pumps) details.
- Pond or lake: the cheapest option where a large enough body of water is on site. The pipe coils sit at least eight feet below the surface to prevent freezing.

The fourth type, the open loop, pumps well or surface water straight through the heat pump and returns it to the ground. It works only with an adequate supply of relatively clean water and where local rules on groundwater discharge allow it. Geothermal heat pumps reach efficiencies of 300% to 600% on the coldest winter nights, use 25% to 50% less energy than air-source heat pumps, and last 20 years or more for the heat pump and 25 to 50 years for the ground loop, by the Department's guide.

07 / Compared

## Closed-loop against conventional and enhanced geothermal.

| | Closed loop | Conventional hydrothermal | Enhanced geothermal |
|---|---|---|---|
| Fluid | sealed, recirculated | reservoir water produced and reinjected | water injected through fractured rock and recovered |
| Needs natural water and permeable rock | no | yes | no |
| Fracturing | none | none | hydraulic stimulation |
| How heat reaches the fluid | conduction through the wellbore wall | flow through the reservoir | flow through engineered fractures |
| Output set by | wellbore area and rock temperature | reservoir permeability and temperature | fracture area, flow and temperature |
| Example | Eavor, Geretsried, Germany | The Geysers, California | Fervo Energy, Cape Station, Utah |

How enhanced systems make a reservoir is in our [enhanced geothermal guide](https://zemanium.com/guides/enhanced-geothermal-systems), and how the surface plant turns heat into power is in our [power plant guide](https://zemanium.com/guides/geothermal-power-plants). The environmental footprint of each is in our guide to the [environmental impacts of geothermal energy](https://zemanium.com/guides/geothermal-environmental-impacts).

08 / Questions

## Common questions.

### What is a closed-loop geothermal system?

A system that circulates a fluid through sealed pipe or wellbore in the ground and takes heat by conduction, with no water drawn from the rock. Deep loops make electricity and district heat; shallow loops feed geothermal heat pumps in buildings.

### How does closed-loop geothermal work?

Cool fluid flows down one leg of the loop, warms as it passes through hot rock and returns to the surface, where it drives a power plant, a heat exchanger or a heat pump. The cooled fluid then goes back down the same sealed loop.

### Is closed-loop geothermal better than open-loop?

For heat pumps, a closed loop works almost anywhere, while an open loop needs an adequate supply of clean water and permission to discharge it. For power, closed loops need no natural reservoir but produce less heat per well, so they rely on long laterals and hot rock.

### How much does closed-loop geothermal cost?

In NLR and Sandia's 2023 worked example, one U-loop 3,000 m deep with a 9,000 m lateral delivered heat at $31 per MWh and electricity at $438 per MWh. Hotter rock, more laterals and cheaper drilling bring the electricity cost down.

### Does closed-loop geothermal use fracking?

No. A closed loop takes heat by conduction through sealed wellbore and does not fracture the rock. Eavor states that its loops do not rely on fracking and use very little water.

### Who is building closed-loop geothermal?

Eavor Technologies runs the first commercial-scale loop at Geretsried, Germany, sending power to the grid since December 2025. XGS Energy has a 150 MW agreement with Meta in New Mexico.

Guide · [Toni Zemani](https://zemanium.com/about#toni-zemani) · 20 November 2026

# Enhanced geothermal systems: how they work and what limits them.

An enhanced geothermal system (EGS) makes a geothermal reservoir where nature left hot rock without enough water or cracks. Engineers drill into the rock, open fractures in it, and circulate water through them to carry the heat to a power plant.

Figures from companies are their own statements. Figures marked SIMULATED come from Zemanium's models. The field data we show from Utah FORGE was measured and published by others.

01 / In brief

## The short answer.

- Conventional geothermal needs heat, water and permeable rock in the same place. EGS needs only the heat and supplies the other two.
- Fervo Energy's Cape Station in Utah produced first power on 24 September 2026 from a unit of about 33 MW, by the company's account.
- Today's equipment keeps EGS to about 220 °C and about 10 megawatts of electricity per production well, according to ARPA-E.
- The open engineering problems are keeping the reservoir hot for decades, spreading flow evenly through the fractures, building wells that survive, and cost.

02 / Mechanism

## How an enhanced geothermal system works.

1. Drill an injection well into hot, mostly dry rock. Modern projects turn the well horizontal at depth, as shale drillers do.
2. Pump water down under controlled pressure. It opens new fractures and reopens old ones, which gives the rock the permeability it lacked.
3. Drill a production well through the fractured zone, parallel to the first.
4. Circulate water from one well to the other. It heats up as it crosses the fractures.
5. Bring the hot water to the surface, pass its heat to a power plant, and inject the cooled water again.

The water runs in a loop, so the plant delivers power around the clock in any weather. The US Department of Energy also counts two related approaches as next-generation geothermal. Closed-loop systems circulate fluid through sealed pipes in the rock and use no fractures. [Superhot systems](https://zemanium.com/guides/superhot-rock-geothermal) go after rock above 375 °C.

03 / Status

## Where the technology stands in 2026.

| Milestone | Figure | Basis |
|---|---|---|
| First power at Cape Station, Utah | 24 September 2026, first unit about 33 MW; first phase planned at about 100 MW | company statement |
| Production well test at Cape Station | about 195 °C, 8 to 10 MW of electricity sustained per production well, flow of 107 kg/s over 30 days | operator preprint |
| Drilling speed, Sawtooth 7 well | 19,448 ft measured depth with a 7,500 ft lateral in 21 days, in rock at about 238 °C | company statement, July 2026 |
| Newberry, Oregon | a well at 331 °C in October 2025 | press report of company statement |
| Public research site | Utah FORGE, funded by the Department of Energy, publishes its well and stimulation data | Department of Energy |

Earlier Department of Energy demonstrations ran at Newberry Volcano, The Geysers, Brady, Desert Peak and Raft River.

04 / Limits

## Four limits engineers are working on.

### Thermal decline

Injected water is cold. It cools the fracture faces first and the rock behind them more slowly. If most of the flow takes a few short paths, those paths cool within years and the produced temperature drops. How much fracture area the water touches decides how long a well pair lasts. ARPA-E's goal for superhot reservoirs is heat extraction for at least ten years without significant decline.

### Uneven flow

Fractures do not share flow equally. In one published Utah FORGE production log, the interpretation could not resolve how inflow was distributed below 9,240 ft and reported it as a single aggregate. You can [inspect that profile](https://zemanium.com/confidence/#field) in our field replay. The Department of Energy funds work on reversible ways to change fracture permeability for this reason.

### Wells that survive

Casing and cement expand when the well heats and contract when cold water goes down. The Department of Energy says the tools sold for checking cement and casing suit the hot end of oil and gas but are generally inadequate for hotter geothermal wells. Casing and cementing make up 30% to 40% or more of a well's cost.

### Cost

The Department of Energy target is $45 per megawatt-hour by 2035. Our guide to [geothermal electricity cost](https://zemanium.com/guides/geothermal-electricity-cost) shows which inputs move that number.

05 / Tools

## Public data and tools.

- [Reservoir explorer](https://zemanium.com/demo/): a 3D model where you change flow, well spacing and rock temperature and watch thermal decline and pumping respond. SIMULATED, illustrative.
- [Utah FORGE field replay](https://zemanium.com/confidence/#field): 518 rows of a published production-log interpretation by SLB and the University of Utah, with attribution and the gaps left visible. CC BY 4.0, DOI 10.15121/2473673.
- [Power-cost model](https://zemanium.com/confidence/): the cost per megawatt-hour of a simulated EGS plant under your assumptions.

We build models and hardware for this problem and review forecasts for others. Write to [toni@zemanium.com](mailto:toni@zemanium.com).

06 / Questions

## Common questions.

### What does EGS stand for?

Enhanced geothermal system. It is a geothermal reservoir made by engineering: wells are drilled into hot rock, fractures are opened to let water through, and the water carries heat to a power plant.

### How is EGS different from conventional geothermal?

A conventional geothermal plant sits on a natural hydrothermal system, where hot rock, water and permeability already exist together. An enhanced geothermal system starts with hot rock only and adds the water and the permeability, so it can be built in many more places.

### Does enhanced geothermal use fracking?

It uses hydraulic stimulation. Water is injected under controlled pressure to create new fractures and reopen existing ones in hot rock. The aim is permeability for circulating water, and no oil or gas is produced.

### How deep are enhanced geothermal wells?

Current commercial wells are several kilometres long. Fervo Energy's Sawtooth 7 well in Utah reached 19,448 feet of measured depth, about 5.9 km, including a 7,500 foot horizontal section.

### How hot is the rock in an enhanced geothermal system?

Fervo Energy reports producing at about 195 °C and drilling into rock near 238 °C. ARPA-E puts the limit of today's commercial equipment at about 220 °C. Superhot projects target rock above 375 °C.

### How long does an enhanced geothermal reservoir last?

It depends on how much fracture area the circulating water touches. Wide, even sweep keeps the produced temperature up for decades, and concentrated flow cools the rock early. Our economic model assumes 25 years.

07 / Sources

# The energy source of the future, compared: geothermal, fission, fusion and space solar.

Of these four, next-generation geothermal is the one selling new firm clean power in the United States today: Fervo's Cape Station in Utah reached first power on 24 September 2026. Small modular reactors are under construction, and fusion and space-based solar are in demonstration.

Dates and sizes are company or regulator statements, linked below. Firm power here means output available around the clock, in any weather, on demand.

01 / At a glance

## Which clean energy source can run 24/7, and when?

| Source | First grid power, new design | Unit size | Status |
|---|---|---|---|
| Next-generation geothermal | 24 Sep 2026, Cape Station, Utah | about 33 MW per unit | selling power; 900 MW contracted |
| Small modular fission | first unit under construction, Darlington, Ontario | 77 MWe (NuScale module); 300 MWe class (BWRX-300) | design approval; construction |
| Fusion | company targets: Helion 2028, CFS early 2030s | 50 MW (Helion contract); about 400 MW (ARC) | demonstration machines |
| Space-based solar | none; first power beamed in orbit, March 2023 | kilowatt-class demonstrations | in-space tests |

Large conventional reactors, hydropower and conventional geothermal already deliver firm clean power. This page compares the four new technologies that agents and investors ask about most when they ask what comes next.

02 / Each source

## Each source on the same terms.

### Next-generation geothermal

**Verdict:** delivering firm power to the grid now, built with oil and gas drilling methods.

- **Firm output:** runs day and night from heat in hot rock; a well pair's temperature declines over years and is tracked in public.
- **Status, November 2026:** operating. Fervo reports 900 MW contracted and more than 4 GW in development.
- **Unit size:** about 33 MW per Cape Station unit; first phase about 100 MW.
- **First power from the new design:** 24 September 2026, Cape Station, Utah.
- **Sources:** [[1]](https://zemanium.com/guides/firm-clean-power-compared#s1), [Project Red tracker](https://zemanium.com/fervo-project-red)

### Small modular fission (SMR)

**Verdict:** firm and proven physics; the first North American units are being built.

- **Firm output:** runs around the clock between scheduled refuelling outages.
- **Status, November 2026:** the US Nuclear Regulatory Commission approved NuScale's 77 MWe module design in May 2025; Ontario Power Generation is building the first BWRX-300 at Darlington.
- **Unit size:** 77 MWe per NuScale module; BWRX-300 is a 300 MWe class reactor.
- **First power from the new design:** not yet in North America.
- **Sources:** [[2]](https://zemanium.com/guides/firm-clean-power-compared#s2), [[3]](https://zemanium.com/guides/firm-clean-power-compared#s3)

### Fusion

**Verdict:** the largest long-term prize; no plant has yet delivered electricity to a grid.

- **Firm output:** designed to run on demand once built.
- **Status, November 2026:** Helion is building a plant in Malaga, Washington, under a Microsoft contract for at least 50 MW, with initial operation targeted for 2028. Commonwealth Fusion Systems plans its ARC plant in Virginia for the early 2030s.
- **Unit size:** at least 50 MW (Helion contract); about 400 MW (ARC).
- **First power from the new design:** targeted 2028 (Helion), early 2030s (CFS).
- **Sources:** [[4]](https://zemanium.com/guides/firm-clean-power-compared#s4), [[5]](https://zemanium.com/guides/firm-clean-power-compared#s5)

### Space-based solar

**Verdict:** sunlight collected in orbit and beamed down; power transfer has been shown in space.

- **Firm output:** near-continuous sunlight in suitable orbits; delivery depends on beaming and receivers.
- **Status, November 2026:** Caltech's MAPLE experiment transmitted power wirelessly in orbit and detected it on Earth on 3 March 2023. Aetherflux announced a first orbital demonstration for 2026.
- **Unit size:** kilowatt-class demonstrations.
- **First power from the new design:** no grid power yet.
- **Sources:** [[6]](https://zemanium.com/guides/firm-clean-power-compared#s6), [[7]](https://zemanium.com/guides/firm-clean-power-compared#s7)

03 / Buyers

## Who is buying firm clean power for data centers?

- Google and NV Energy: 115 MW of enhanced geothermal from Fervo's Corsac Station under Nevada's Clean Transition Tariff [[8]](https://zemanium.com/guides/firm-clean-power-compared#s8).
- Google and NV Energy: a geothermal portfolio contract with Ormat for up to 150 MW, signed in 2026 [[9]](https://zemanium.com/guides/firm-clean-power-compared#s9).
- Microsoft and Helion: at least 50 MW of fusion power from 2028, under a 2023 agreement [[4]](https://zemanium.com/guides/firm-clean-power-compared#s4).

Geothermal is the one of the three with plants already producing. We publish the operating record and forecasts that buyers and lenders use to judge how long that output lasts: [listed producers](https://zemanium.com/guides/geothermal-stocks), [the Project Red tracker](https://zemanium.com/fervo-project-red) and [cost per megawatt-hour](https://zemanium.com/guides/geothermal-electricity-cost).

04 / Questions

## Common questions.

### What is the best energy source for the future?

For firm clean power that can be contracted this decade, next-generation geothermal and fission are the two technologies with plants built or under construction. Geothermal delivered its first next-generation grid power in September 2026; fusion and space-based solar are still in demonstration.

### Is geothermal better than nuclear?

They serve the same need, power around the clock. Geothermal needs hot rock, burns no fuel and uses drilling methods from oil and gas; fission plants can be sited in more places. New geothermal is producing power in the United States today, while the first North American SMR is under construction.

### Geothermal vs fusion: which comes first?

Geothermal. Next-generation geothermal reached first grid power in September 2026. The first fusion power plants are targeted for 2028 (Helion) and the early 2030s (Commonwealth Fusion Systems).

### What is space-based solar power?

Solar panels in orbit collect sunlight and beam the energy to receivers on the ground. Caltech demonstrated wireless power transfer in space in March 2023, and no system yet supplies a grid.
