# Geothermal companies in 2026: who is building what.

Most geothermal power today comes from long-established operators such as Ormat in the United States, Pertamina Geothermal Energy in Indonesia and KenGen in Kenya. A newer group is adding enhanced, closed-loop and superhot geothermal: Fervo Energy's Cape Station in Utah sent its first power on 24 September 2026, Eavor's closed-loop plant in Germany has delivered power since December 2025, and Sage Geosystems, XGS Energy, Zanskar, Quaise Energy and Mazama Energy have plants under way.

Milestones are the companies' own statements or press reports of them, dated and linked below. Capacity figures for listed producers are company statements. Independent summary; not investment advice. Zemanium holds no position in any security.

01 / Developers

## Which companies are building next-generation geothermal?

| Company | Approach | Latest milestone | Basis |
|---|---|---|---|
| Fervo Energy (Nasdaq: FRVO) | enhanced geothermal with horizontal wells and hydraulic stimulation | Cape Station, Utah, first power 24 September 2026 from a first unit of about 33 MW, in a 500 MW multi-phase project; Project Red pilot in Nevada since 2023 | company statements; EnergyTech and Canary Media, 2026 [[1]](https://zemanium.com/guides/geothermal-companies#s1) [[2]](https://zemanium.com/guides/geothermal-companies#s2) [[3]](https://zemanium.com/guides/geothermal-companies#s3) |
| Sage Geosystems | enhanced geothermal that stores water under pressure in fractures | 3 MW pilot near San Antonio, Texas, selling power since April 2026; next well at an Ormat plant in Nevada; 150 MW agreement with Meta | Canary Media, 19 August 2026 [[3]](https://zemanium.com/guides/geothermal-companies#s3) |
| XGS Energy | solid-state geothermal system built on thermally conductive materials | 150 MW agreement with Meta in New Mexico; engineering services from Baker Hughes; ARPA-E SUPERHOT award of $3.0m, November 2026 | company statements; ARPA-E [[4]](https://zemanium.com/guides/geothermal-companies#s4) [[9]](https://zemanium.com/guides/geothermal-companies#s9) |
| Zanskar | AI-guided exploration for hidden natural hydrothermal systems | $115m Series C, January 2026; 100 MW power purchase agreement with NV Energy for delivery by 2030; DOE field test selection, September 2026 | company statements; Renewable Energy Magazine [[5]](https://zemanium.com/guides/geothermal-companies#s5) [[6]](https://zemanium.com/guides/geothermal-companies#s6) [[2]](https://zemanium.com/guides/geothermal-companies#s2) |
| Eavor Technologies | closed loop: sealed multilateral wells, no fracturing or water from the rock | Geretsried, Germany, first power to the grid December 2025; 12 laterals, 16 km of wellbore per pair | company statement [[7]](https://zemanium.com/guides/geothermal-companies#s7) |
| Quaise Energy | millimetre-wave drilling into superhot rock | Project Obsidian, Oregon, 50 MW, power targeted by 2030; up to $25m from DOE, September 2026; $180m Series B, August 2026 | company statements; EnergyTech [[2]](https://zemanium.com/guides/geothermal-companies#s2) [[8]](https://zemanium.com/guides/geothermal-companies#s8) |
| Mazama Energy | superhot enhanced geothermal, drill bits cooled with carbon dioxide | well at 331 °C at Newberry, Oregon, in October 2025 and a later well above 700 °F; $135m raised, September 2026 | TechCrunch, 16 November 2026 [[10]](https://zemanium.com/guides/geothermal-companies#s10) |

The approaches differ in how they get heat out of the rock. Our guides explain [enhanced geothermal systems](https://zemanium.com/guides/enhanced-geothermal-systems) and [superhot rock geothermal](https://zemanium.com/guides/superhot-rock-geothermal), and the [wells guide](https://zemanium.com/guides/geothermal-wells) compares their drilling records.

03 / Utilities and suppliers

## Utilities, operators and oilfield suppliers.

- Large utilities such as Enel and Berkshire Hathaway Energy own geothermal plants as a small part of wider fleets. In Nevada's regulator record Enel is the operator of record at Salt Wells and Stillwater.
- Geysers Power Company, a subsidiary of Calpine, runs The Geysers in California, which NLR calls the most prolific geothermal field in the United States.
- Oilfield service companies sell into geothermal wells: Baker Hughes is providing engineering for XGS Energy's New Mexico project, and SLB interpreted Utah FORGE's production logs for the Department of Energy.

04 / Buyers

## Who is buying next-generation geothermal power?

Data center owners and utilities. Meta has agreements for 150 MW each with Sage Geosystems and XGS Energy. Fervo built its Project Red pilot in partnership with Google, according to Canary Media. NV Energy signed a 20-year agreement with Zanskar for 100 MW by 2030. Public geothermal power contracts signed between November 2019 and June 2025 priced at $67.50 to $99 per megawatt-hour, according to the National Laboratory of the Rockies.

05 / Zemanium

## Where Zemanium fits.

Zemanium is a geothermal invention lab working on the well itself: casing and cement that survive the heating and cooling cycles of superhot wells, and Pandora, a casing joint for wells at 450 to 500 °C. We also publish open records for the whole field: a monthly [Project Red tracker](https://zemanium.com/fervo-project-red) scored against the Nevada regulator, Nevada plant and field data, and an [LCOE calculator](https://zemanium.com/lcoe-calculator). Developers, operators and investors who want an independent review of a well or reservoir forecast can write to [toni@zemanium.com](mailto:toni@zemanium.com).

06 / Questions

## Common questions.

### What are the biggest geothermal companies?

By installed capacity, Pertamina Geothermal Energy reports 1,932 MW in Indonesia including partner-operated plants, and Ormat Technologies a 1,853 MW portfolio that includes solar and storage. KenGen runs 754 MW of geothermal in Kenya.

### What companies are doing enhanced geothermal?

Fervo Energy, which reached first power at Cape Station in Utah on 24 September 2026, Sage Geosystems, with a 3 MW pilot in Texas, and Mazama Energy, drilling superhot wells in Oregon. The Department of Energy selected Fervo, Zanskar, AlterG Resources, Quaise Energy and the University of Utah for field-scale enhanced geothermal tests in September 2026.

### Is Fervo Energy a public company?

Yes. Fervo Energy trades on Nasdaq under the ticker FRVO after pricing its initial public offering at $27 a share on 12 May 2026.

### What is closed-loop geothermal?

A system that circulates fluid through sealed wells in hot rock and takes heat by conduction, with no fracturing and no water drawn from the rock. Eavor's plant at Geretsried, Germany, connects 12 lateral wells into six pairs and has sent power to the grid since December 2025, by the company's account. Our [closed-loop geothermal guide](https://zemanium.com/guides/closed-loop-geothermal) has its results and costs.

### Which geothermal startups have raised the most money?

Among the developers on this page, Quaise Energy closed a $180m Series B in August 2026, Mazama Energy raised $135m in September 2026, and Zanskar raised a $115m Series C in January 2026, bringing its equity to $180m. Fervo Energy raised public equity in its May 2026 listing.

### Which geothermal companies are in the USA?

Fervo Energy in Utah and Nevada, Sage Geosystems in Texas, XGS Energy in New Mexico, Zanskar with a power agreement with NV Energy, and Quaise Energy and Mazama Energy in Oregon, among the developers. Ormat Technologies and Calpine, operator of The Geysers in California, run the largest existing US fleets.

Guide · [Toni Zemani](https://zemanium.com/about#toni-zemani) · 20 November 2026, updated 27 November 2026

# What geothermal electricity costs in 2026, and what sets the price.

New geothermal power costs $67 to $111 per megawatt-hour before subsidies, by Lazard's 2026 estimate, close to new utility solar at $40 to $98 and onshore wind at $37 to $99. A geothermal plant is paid for almost entirely before it produces anything, so that price depends on four things: what the wells cost, how much power each well delivers, how long that output lasts, and the interest rate on the money.

Numbers marked SIMULATED come from our own model and are scenarios built on assumptions. They are requirements for a design, and no plant has been built to them. Numbers from other organisations are quoted with their source.

01 / In brief

## How much does geothermal electricity cost?

- New geothermal plants: $67 to $111 per megawatt-hour unsubsidized, average $89, in Lazard's 2026 Levelized Cost of Energy+ (version 19.0).
- Signed contracts: public geothermal power purchase agreements from November 2019 to June 2025 priced at $67.50 to $99 per megawatt-hour, for 10 to 30 years, as compiled in the 2025 Annual Technology Baseline of the National Laboratory of the Rockies (NLR, formerly NREL).
- The US Department of Energy wants enhanced geothermal power at $45 per megawatt-hour by 2035, about 90% below where the technology stood in 2022. ARPA-E's SUPERHOT program aims under $30 for wells above 375 °C by 2040.
- In our own model the same simulated plant costs $83.02, $43.35 or $35.00 per megawatt-hour depending on its capital cost and discount rate. The rock and the wells are identical in all three cases.
- Zemanium's development target is $30 to $45 per megawatt-hour. It is what our hardware program is designed toward.

02 / Build cost

## What a geothermal power plant and its wells cost.

| Item | Figure | Source |
|---|---|---|
| New-build geothermal plant, capital cost | $5,135 to $6,635 per kW | Lazard LCOE+ 2026 |
| Illustrative next-generation geothermal plant | $7,000 per kW, fixed O&M $160 per kW-year | Lazard LCOE+ 2026, from public estimates |
| Hydrothermal flash sites at 200 °C or hotter, identified in the US | average $4,362 per kW overnight capital cost | NLR, Annual Technology Baseline 2025 |
| Deep enhanced geothermal, example flash plant | $6,653 per kW | NLR, Annual Technology Baseline 2025 |
| Drilling share of a new plant's capital cost | 30% to 57% | NLR, 2025 drilling cost curves |
| Fervo Cape Station, cost per well | down from $9.4 million to $4.8 million | company statement, reported April 2024 |
| Cost per foot drilled, Project Red pilot wells | $995 and $1,107 | NLR, 2025 drilling cost curves |
| Cost per foot drilled, first six Cape Station wells (2023 to 2024) | $634 falling to $346 | NLR, 2025 drilling cost curves |

A 13,000 foot well at $346 to $634 a foot costs about $4.5 million to $8.2 million to drill, before completion. Our [guide to geothermal wells](https://zemanium.com/guides/geothermal-wells) covers depth, drilling records and how long wells keep their temperature.

03 / Method

## How LCOE is calculated.

The levelized cost of electricity (LCOE) is the price per megawatt-hour at which a plant pays back everything spent on it over its life, including the return its lenders and owners expect. It divides discounted lifetime cost by discounted lifetime output:

`LCOE = sum of (cost in year t / (1 + r)^t) / sum of (electricity exported in year t / (1 + r)^t)`

Here `r` is the discount rate and `t` runs from construction to the last operating year. For geothermal the largest costs fall in year zero: drilling, completing the wells and building the power plant. Fuel is free. That makes the answer sensitive to the discount rate and to how long the wells keep their output.

Use exported electricity in the denominator. A geothermal plant spends some of its own output on pumps and auxiliaries, and an LCOE computed on gross generation flatters the plant. Our model exports gross generation minus pumping minus 5% of gross for auxiliaries.

04 / Targets

## Published cost targets.

| Who | Target | By | Applies to |
|---|---|---|---|
| US Department of Energy, Enhanced Geothermal Shot | $45/MWh | 2035 | enhanced geothermal systems |
| ARPA-E, SUPERHOT program | under $30/MWh | 2040 | reservoirs above 375 °C and 22 MPa, 10 to 20 GW |
| Zemanium | $30 to $45/MWh | development target, no date claimed | our hardware and well program |

The analysis behind the Department of Energy figure put developed deep enhanced geothermal at $45.60 per megawatt-hour in 2035, rounded to $45. All three rows are goals.

05 / Worked example

## One simulated plant, three prices.

Our power-cost model holds the physics fixed and changes only the money. The reservoir starts at 200 °C, runs for 25 simulated years, and feeds a plant sized to its peak output of 28.322 MW gross.

| Case | Capital assumptions | Real discount rate | LCOE |
|---|---|---|---|
| Reference | reference plant and well costs | 8% | $83.02/MWh |
| Target package | $1,500 per gross kW plant, $15m subsurface, $3m other | 8% | $43.35/MWh |
| Target package, cheaper money | same | 4% | $35.00/MWh |

SIMULATED · assumption scenarios · 5 October 2026

Halving the cost of capital takes $8.35 off each megawatt-hour without touching a single piece of equipment. Getting from $83.02 to $43.35 needs the plant and the wells to cost roughly what the target package says. No supplier has quoted those prices. They tell us what our hardware has to achieve.

The model runs 1,080 cost scenarios on output trajectories from GEOPHIRES-X 3.18.3, the open source simulator from NREL. It charges 2% of installed capital a year for operations, make-up water and $8 per exported megawatt-hour, books a $5m event in year 12 and $2m in year 25, and assumes the plant runs 90% of the time. A stress test draws 2,000 combinations of discount rate (4% to 12%), capital overrun (0.8 to 1.2 times) and a mid-life replacement of up to $10m.

06 / Drivers

## What moves the cost.

### Wells

The Department of Energy calls lower well construction cost a requirement for expanding enhanced geothermal, and puts casing and cementing alone at 30% to 40% or more of what a well costs. Drilling time is falling: Fervo Energy reports reaching 19,448 feet of measured depth in 21 days on its Sawtooth 7 well in July 2026.

### Power per well

A well that produces twice the power halves the drilling bill per megawatt. ARPA-E says today's equipment limits enhanced geothermal to about 220 °C and about 10 megawatts of electricity per production well, and that wells above 375 °C could reach 30 to 50. That gap is why developers want [superhot rock](https://zemanium.com/guides/superhot-rock-geothermal).

### How long the output lasts

Cold water injected into hot rock cools the rock it touches. If the water sweeps a small volume, the produced temperature falls early and every later year earns less. Our model includes a case that fails this way: with the reservoir volume cut from 1 cubic kilometre to 0.014, the plant ends up importing power, and we publish no price for it.

### Cost of capital

Because nearly all spending comes first, the discount rate acts on the whole bill. The example above moves 19% between 8% and 4%.

### The plant on the surface

Hotter fluid converts a larger share of its heat to electricity, so a 200 °C plant needs more equipment per kilowatt than a hotter one. The model lets you set installed plant cost from $1,500 to $4,500 per gross kilowatt.

07 / Tool

## Run the model yourself.

For a quick estimate with your own numbers, the [LCOE calculator](https://zemanium.com/lcoe-calculator) takes capital cost, operating cost, capacity factor, life and discount rate for any power plant. The [power-cost model](https://zemanium.com/confidence/) goes further for geothermal and runs in your browser with no account. Set the plant cost, subsurface cost, discount rate and a target price, and it returns the LCOE and the capital the design can afford. It also shows the cases that fail. The 3D [reservoir explorer](https://zemanium.com/demo/) shows how flow, well spacing and rock temperature change thermal decline and pumping.

If you want this analysis for a specific project, or an independent review of a forecast, write to [toni@zemanium.com](mailto:toni@zemanium.com).

08 / Questions

## Common questions.

### Is geothermal energy expensive?

It costs more to build and less to run than most sources. Lazard puts new geothermal at $67 to $111 per megawatt-hour in 2026, against $40 to $98 for utility solar and $37 to $99 for onshore wind, and geothermal runs day and night. Almost all of the cost is drilling and plant construction paid up front.

### How is the LCOE of a geothermal plant calculated?

Add up every cost over the plant's life, discount each year's cost back to today, and divide by the discounted electricity exported over the same years. Subtract pumping and auxiliary power from generation first, because the plant consumes them itself.

### How much does a geothermal well cost?

Fervo Energy reported its Cape Station wells falling from $9.4 million to $4.8 million each. NLR's 2025 analysis puts the first six Cape Station wells at $346 to $634 per foot drilled, and drilling at 30% to 57% of a new plant's capital cost. Our model treats the whole subsurface scope as an allowance of $15m, $25m or $37m per case.

### How much does a geothermal power plant cost?

Lazard's 2026 range for a new plant is $5,135 to $6,635 per kilowatt of capacity, so a 50 MW plant costs roughly $257 million to $332 million. NLR's 2025 baseline averages $4,362 per kilowatt for hot hydrothermal sites and gives $6,653 for an example deep enhanced geothermal plant.

### Is there a free geothermal LCOE calculator?

Yes. The Zemanium [LCOE calculator](https://zemanium.com/lcoe-calculator) prices any plant from capital cost, operating cost, capacity factor, life and discount rate, and the power-cost model at zemanium.com/confidence prices a simulated geothermal plant. Both run in a browser and need no account. For full reservoir and plant simulation, GEOPHIRES-X is open source.

### Why does the discount rate matter so much for geothermal?

Nearly all the money is spent before the first megawatt-hour is sold, so the financing cost applies to almost the whole budget. In our simulated example the same plant costs $43.35 per megawatt-hour at an 8% real discount rate and $35.00 at 4%.

Guide · [Toni Zemani](https://zemanium.com/about#toni-zemani) · 27 November 2026

# Geothermal energy pros and cons, with the numbers behind each.

Geothermal power runs day and night: US plants ran at a 65.9% capacity factor in 2025, against 24.0% for solar and 33.8% for wind. It emits about 99% less carbon dioxide than fossil plants and burns no fuel. Its drawbacks are a high up-front drilling bill, a limited number of naturally hot, wet sites, reservoirs that cool over a plant's life, and earthquakes from stimulating rock.

Each point carries its source. Capacity factors are measured by the US Energy Information Administration; costs are Lazard and NLR estimates; Nevada field temperatures are measured and operator-reported to the state regulator, and the field averages are computed by Zemanium.

01 / Summary

## What are the pros and cons of geothermal energy?

| Pros | Evidence | Cons | Evidence |
|---|---|---|---|
| Runs day and night in any weather | 65.9% US capacity factor, 2025 (EIA) | High up-front cost | drilling is 30% to 57% of a new plant's capital cost (NLR) |
| Very low emissions | about 99% less CO2 and 97% less sulfur compounds than fossil plants (EIA) | Exploration risk | baseline exploration drilling success rate 60% (NLR) |
| No fuel to buy | contracts at $67.50 to $99 per MWh fixed for 10 to 30 years (NLR) | Limited natural sites | most US plants sit in western states and Hawaii (EIA) |
| Plants last for decades | The Geysers has produced power since 1960 (EIA) | Reservoirs can cool | 11 of 18 long-running Nevada fields produce cooler fluid than in their first year (regulator record) |
| Huge resource with new technology | about 7,500 GW of enhanced geothermal potential in the US (DOE analysis via NLR) | Induced earthquakes | a magnitude 5.5 earthquake at Pohang, South Korea, in 2017 was triggered by stimulation (Ellsworth and others, 2019) |

02 / Advantages

## What are the advantages of geothermal energy?

### It produces power around the clock

Heat underground does not depend on sun or wind. In 2025 the US geothermal fleet ran at a 65.9% capacity factor, meaning it produced 65.9% of what its available capacity could have delivered running flat out all year. Utility solar ran at 24.0%, wind at 33.8% and nuclear at 91.1%, by the EIA's count. Lazard models new geothermal plants at 80% to 90%.

### It emits very little

Geothermal plants burn nothing. The EIA puts their emissions at about 99% less carbon dioxide and about 97% less sulfur compounds than fossil fuel plants. Binary-cycle plants pass the hot water through a heat exchanger and send it back underground, so they produce no air emissions at all.

### The fuel is free and the price is fixed

Once the wells are drilled the heat costs nothing, so geothermal power sells on long fixed contracts. Public US agreements signed between November 2019 and June 2025 priced at $67.50 to $99 per megawatt-hour for 10 to 30 years, as compiled by the National Laboratory of the Rockies (NLR, formerly NREL).

### Plants run for decades

The first geothermal power plant ran in Italy in 1904, and The Geysers in California has produced electricity since 1960, according to the EIA. NLR's cost baseline assumes a 30-year life for plant and reservoir.

### The resource is enormous once drilling gets cheaper

Natural hot-water systems are rare, but hot rock is everywhere at depth. The US Department of Energy's Enhanced Geothermal Shot analysis estimated about 7,500 GW of enhanced geothermal potential in the United States, against about 2,700 MW of geothermal capacity running in 2025. Our guide to [enhanced geothermal systems](https://zemanium.com/guides/enhanced-geothermal-systems) explains how that rock is put to work.

03 / Disadvantages

## What are the disadvantages of geothermal energy?

### Most of the money is spent before the first megawatt-hour

Lazard's 2026 estimate for a new geothermal plant is $5,135 to $6,635 per kilowatt, against $1,250 to $1,850 for utility solar. Drilling accounts for 30% to 57% of the capital cost, by NLR's 2025 analysis. That makes the price of geothermal power sensitive to interest rates; our [cost guide](https://zemanium.com/guides/geothermal-electricity-cost) shows by how much.

### Wells can come up dry

A geothermal field is proven only by drilling into it. NLR's 2025 baseline assumes 60% of exploration wells at a new hydrothermal site succeed, in line with a global average of 59% recorded in 2013. Each miss costs millions of dollars.

### Natural sites are limited

A conventional plant needs heat, water and permeable rock in the same place. That combination sits mostly near tectonic plate edges, and most US plants are in western states and Hawaii, according to the EIA. Enhanced and closed-loop systems are built to work without the natural water and cracks.

### Reservoirs cool during a plant's life

Cold water injected back into the rock cools it over time. Nevada publishes the temperature of every producing well each month. Across 18 fields with ten or more years of record, the flow-weighted produced temperature fell by more than 5 °F in 11, held within 5 °F in 3 and rose in 4. At Blue Mountain it fell from 368 °F in 2009 to 281 °F in 2025. Fervo's Project Red well pair went from 347 °F in 2024 to 316 °F in July 2026. Operators answer with new wells, which is a running cost. The field-by-field table is in our guide [is geothermal energy renewable](https://zemanium.com/guides/is-geothermal-energy-renewable).

### Stimulating rock can trigger earthquakes

Enhanced systems open fractures with water under pressure, and that can set off earthquakes. In November 2017 a magnitude 5.5 earthquake struck Pohang, South Korea, injuring 135 people; a government-appointed research committee concluded it was triggered by stimulation at an enhanced geothermal pilot. Fervo Energy's 2026 Department of Energy award in Idaho includes a high-temperature geophone array to monitor this.

### Some plants release gases

Geothermal fluid carries hydrogen sulfide and small amounts of carbon dioxide. Plants use scrubbers to remove the hydrogen sulfide, and most inject the steam and water back into the ground, according to the EIA. Emissions, water use and induced earthquakes are measured side by side in our guide to the [environmental impacts of geothermal energy](https://zemanium.com/guides/geothermal-environmental-impacts).

04 / Compared

## Geothermal against other power sources.

| Source | US capacity factor, 2025 | New-build cost, 2026, $/MWh unsubsidized | Runs at night |
|---|---|---|---|
| Geothermal | 65.9% | $67 to $111 | yes |
| Solar PV, utility | 24.0% | $40 to $98 | no |
| Wind, onshore | 33.8% | $37 to $99 | when the wind blows |
| Nuclear | 91.1% | $175 to $255 | yes |
| Gas, combined cycle | 58.7% | $51 to $129 | yes, with fuel |

Capacity factors from EIA Electric Power Monthly tables 6.07.A and 6.07.B; costs from Lazard's Levelized Cost of Energy+ version 19.0. Our [firm clean power comparison](https://zemanium.com/guides/firm-clean-power-compared) sets geothermal against small reactors, fusion and space solar.

05 / Outlook

## Which disadvantages new technology is working on.

- Drilling cost. Fervo Energy reported its Cape Station wells falling from $9.4 million to $4.8 million each, and NLR's 2025 cost curves cut 12% to 26% from the 2017 baseline. More in our [guide to geothermal wells](https://zemanium.com/guides/geothermal-wells).
- Location. Enhanced geothermal reached commercial power at Cape Station, Utah, on 24 September 2026, by Fervo's account. Eavor's closed-loop plant at Geretsried, Germany, has sent power to the grid since December 2025.
- Power per well. Wells in superhot rock above 375 °C could deliver 30 to 50 MW each against about 10 today, according to ARPA-E. Their steel casing is the limit; that is our work, described in the [superhot rock guide](https://zemanium.com/guides/superhot-rock-geothermal).
- Cooling. Wider, even flow through more fractures uses more rock and slows cooling. Our [Project Red tracker](https://zemanium.com/fervo-project-red) scores a registered forecast of one well pair against the regulator record every month.

The companies doing this work are listed in our [guide to geothermal companies](https://zemanium.com/guides/geothermal-companies).

06 / Questions

## Common questions.

### What is the biggest disadvantage of geothermal energy?

Up-front cost. Drilling makes up 30% to 57% of a new plant's capital cost, and the whole plant is paid for before it sells power. Lazard puts new geothermal at $5,135 to $6,635 per kilowatt, several times the cost of utility solar per kilowatt.

### What is the main advantage of geothermal energy?

It delivers clean power day and night. US geothermal plants ran at a 65.9% capacity factor in 2025, against 24.0% for solar and 33.8% for wind, while emitting about 99% less carbon dioxide than fossil plants.

### Is geothermal energy bad for the environment?

Its effects are small next to fossil fuels. Plants emit about 99% less carbon dioxide and 97% less sulfur compounds, scrub hydrogen sulfide and reinject their water. The local risks are induced earthquakes from stimulation and the land and water used at the site.

### Why is geothermal energy not used more?

Conventional plants need rare spots where heat, water and permeable rock meet, and drilling is expensive and risky. Enhanced and closed-loop systems remove the need for natural water and cracks, and their drilling costs fell sharply between 2022 and 2025.

### Can geothermal energy run out?

The Earth's heat will not run out, but a single reservoir can cool when heat is drawn faster than the rock refills it. In Nevada, 11 of 18 long-running fields produced cooler fluid in 2025 than in their first recorded year.

### Does geothermal energy cause earthquakes?

Stimulating rock for enhanced systems can trigger earthquakes. A government-appointed committee linked the magnitude 5.5 Pohang earthquake of 2017 in South Korea to stimulation at an enhanced geothermal pilot. Fervo Energy's 2026 Department of Energy award in Idaho includes a high-temperature geophone array to monitor seismicity.

# The environmental impacts of geothermal energy, measured.

Geothermal power has one of the smallest environmental footprints of any electricity source. Over its whole life it emits a median 37 grams of CO2-equivalent per kilowatt-hour, against 486 for natural gas and 1,001 for coal, by the 2021 review of the National Laboratory of the Rockies. Its local impacts are gases carried up in the fluid, water use, small induced earthquakes and, where fluid is drawn out and not replaced, sinking ground. Each has a working control: scrubbers, reinjection, dry cooling and seismic monitoring.

Figures are quoted from the EIA, the National Laboratory of the Rockies (NLR, formerly NREL), the World Bank's ESMAP programme, the USGS, peer-reviewed papers and company statements, each named where it appears. Work-per-kilogram figures are Zemanium model results, labelled [MODEL].

01 / Summary

## What are the environmental impacts of geothermal energy?

| Impact | What causes it | How large | How plants control it |
|---|---|---|---|
| Greenhouse gases | carbon dioxide dissolved in the reservoir fluid, plus building the plant and drilling | median 37 g CO2e/kWh over the life cycle (NLR) | binary plants and full reinjection keep the gas underground |
| Air pollutants | hydrogen sulfide in the steam | about 97% less sulfur compounds than fossil fuel plants (EIA) | scrubbers |
| Water use | evaporation in cooling towers and fluid lost in the reservoir | 5 to 505 gallons per MWh by plant type (Macknick and colleagues) | dry cooling and reinjection |
| Induced earthquakes | injection, withdrawal and stimulation change the stress on small faults | mostly small; the largest at The Geysers is about magnitude 4.5 (USGS) | seismic monitoring and injection limits |
| Sinking ground | pressure falls when fluid is drawn out and not replaced | about 15 m at the centre of the Wairakei bowl, New Zealand, by 2009 | reinjection to hold reservoir pressure |
| Natural features | drawing on the same hot water that feeds geysers and hot springs | site-specific | legal protection at places such as Yellowstone (EIA) |

Direct use of geothermal heat and geothermal heat pumps have almost no negative effects on the environment, by the EIA's account. The impacts in this guide are those of geothermal power plants.

02 / Emissions

## How much CO2 does geothermal energy emit?

A median 37 grams of CO2-equivalent per kilowatt-hour over the whole life cycle: building the plant, drilling, operation and decommissioning. That sits beside solar and far below fossil fuels in NLR's 2021 review of published life-cycle studies:

| Source | Median life-cycle emissions (g CO2e/kWh) |
|---|---|
| Coal | 1,001 |
| Oil | 840 |
| Natural gas | 486 |
| Solar photovoltaic | 43 |
| Geothermal | 37 |
| Concentrating solar | 28 |
| Hydropower | 21 |
| Wind | 13 |
| Nuclear | 13 |

Operating emissions depend on the field, because the carbon dioxide comes from the rock and the fluid, not from burning anything. The World Bank's ESMAP programme reports a global weighted average of 122 g/kWh from a 2001 survey of operating plants, and measured 400 to 1,300 g/kWh at plants in Turkey. Binary plants pass the heat through a closed heat exchanger and inject all the fluid back underground, so they have no air emissions, according to the EIA. Across the fleet, geothermal plants emit about 99% less carbon dioxide than fossil fuel plants, by the EIA's count.

03 / Pollution

## Does geothermal energy cause pollution?

Very little. A geothermal plant burns no fuel, so it makes no smoke, soot or ash. The pollutant to manage is hydrogen sulfide, a gas in the steam that smells of rotten eggs. Plants remove it with scrubbers, and the EIA puts geothermal plants at about 97% less of the sulfur compounds that cause acid rain than fossil fuel plants.

The water that comes up carries dissolved minerals and salts. Most plants inject the steam and water they use back into the earth, which keeps those minerals underground, renews the resource and further reduces emissions, according to the EIA.

04 / Water

## How much water does a geothermal power plant use?

It depends on the plant type and its cooling. The review of operational water consumption by Macknick and colleagues gives these medians:

| Plant | Cooling | Water consumed, gallons per MWh (median) | Range |
|---|---|---|---|
| Geothermal flash | dry | 5 | one study |
| Geothermal flash | cooling tower | 15 | 5 to 361 |
| Geothermal binary | dry | 270 | one study |
| Geothermal binary | hybrid | 461 | 221 to 700 |
| Enhanced geothermal | dry | 505 | 290 to 720 |
| Natural gas combined cycle | cooling tower | 205 | 130 to 300 |
| Nuclear | cooling tower | 672 | 581 to 845 |
| Coal | cooling tower | 687 | 480 to 1,100 |

A flash plant with a cooling tower consumes a fraction of the water of a gas, nuclear or coal plant with the same cooling. Enhanced systems also need water to stimulate the rock, which is why they sit at the top of the geothermal range.

05 / Earthquakes

## Does geothermal energy cause earthquakes?

It can cause small ones. At The Geysers in California, the withdrawal of steam and the injection of cold water induce small earthquakes that workers and nearby residents often feel. The USGS reports that seismicity there has been fairly stable since the mid-1980s, that the largest quake recorded at the field is about magnitude 4.5, and that much larger ones are thought unlikely because no large continuous fault runs through the field.

Stimulating hot rock for an enhanced system carries the larger risk. In November 2017 a magnitude 5.5 earthquake struck Pohang, South Korea; Ellsworth and colleagues showed in 2019 that stimulation at an enhanced geothermal pilot triggered it. Projects now follow induced-seismicity protocols such as the US Department of Energy's of 2012: screen the site, monitor in real time and adjust or stop injection when quakes pass agreed thresholds. Fervo Energy publishes its own approach to managing induced seismicity.

06 / Ground

## Can geothermal energy make the ground sink?

Yes, where fluid is drawn out faster than it is replaced and reservoir pressure falls. At Wairakei in New Zealand, which has produced power since 1958, the centre of the main subsidence bowl had sunk about 15 m by 2009, at a peak rate of 498 mm a year in 1979, by the account of Brockbank and colleagues. Injecting the fluid back holds reservoir pressure up, and most geothermal plants now do it, according to the EIA.

07 / Heat pumps

## Geothermal heat pumps and the environment.

Geothermal heat pumps move heat between a building and the ground through sealed loops of pipe. They can use 25% to 50% less energy than air-source heat pumps, by the US Department of Energy's guide, and the EIA counts them among the geothermal uses with almost no negative effects on the environment. Our guide to [closed-loop geothermal](https://zemanium.com/guides/closed-loop-geothermal) explains the loop types.

08 / New designs

## How newer geothermal designs change the footprint.

- Closed-loop systems circulate their own fluid through sealed wells and exchange no water with the rock by design. At Geretsried, Germany, Eavor's first loop lost 0.5% to 2% of its circulating fluid to the rock, and the company expects about 0.1% in deeper, tighter basement rock.
- Enhanced systems open fractures in hot dry rock, which raises water use and calls for seismic monitoring. More in our [enhanced geothermal guide](https://zemanium.com/guides/enhanced-geothermal-systems).
- Hotter fluid does more work per kilogram. At 400 °C a kilogram of fluid can deliver 566 to 617 kJ of work, against 172 kJ at 200 °C, so a plant on 400 °C fluid lifts and reinjects less than a third as much fluid for the same work. That is the case for [superhot rock geothermal](https://zemanium.com/guides/superhot-rock-geothermal).

[MODEL] · IAPWS water properties · 27 November 2026

Where these resources lie is on our [geothermal map](https://zemanium.com/guides/geothermal-map), and the trade-offs beyond the environment are in our guide to [geothermal energy pros and cons](https://zemanium.com/guides/geothermal-energy-pros-and-cons).

09 / Questions

## Common questions.

### What are the environmental impacts of geothermal energy?

Low carbon emissions, a median 37 g CO2e per kWh over the life cycle, and four local impacts: hydrogen sulfide in the steam, water use of 5 to 505 gallons per MWh by plant type, small induced earthquakes and, where fluid is not reinjected, sinking ground.

### Does geothermal energy cause pollution?

Very little. Plants burn no fuel, scrub hydrogen sulfide from the steam and emit about 97% less sulfur compounds and 99% less carbon dioxide than fossil fuel plants, according to the EIA. Binary plants have no air emissions.

### Is geothermal energy clean?

Yes. Its median life-cycle emissions of 37 g CO2e per kWh are close to solar photovoltaic at 43 and about a thirteenth of natural gas at 486, by NLR's 2021 review.

### Does geothermal energy cause earthquakes?

Sometimes, and mostly small ones. The largest recorded at The Geysers in California is about magnitude 4.5, according to the USGS. Stimulation at an enhanced geothermal pilot triggered the magnitude 5.5 Pohang earthquake in South Korea in 2017, and projects now monitor seismicity and limit injection.

### How much water does geothermal energy use?

From about 5 gallons per MWh for a dry-cooled flash plant to 505 for an enhanced system, by the review of Macknick and colleagues, against 672 for a nuclear plant and 687 for a coal plant with cooling towers.

### What are the problems with geothermal energy?

For the environment: gases in the steam, water use, induced earthquakes and sinking ground, controlled by scrubbers, dry cooling, monitoring and reinjection. For the business: high upfront drilling cost and the risk of dry wells, both covered in our [pros and cons guide](https://zemanium.com/guides/geothermal-energy-pros-and-cons).

Guide · [Toni Zemani](https://zemanium.com/about#toni-zemani) · 27 November 2026

# The geothermal gradient: how much hotter the Earth gets with depth.

The geothermal gradient is the rate at which rock temperature rises with depth. In most continental crust away from plate boundaries it is about 25 to 30 °C per kilometre. It varies with the heat flowing up from below and with the rock: across the United States it runs from 15 to 35 °C per kilometre, averaging 25 in the east and 34 in the west. On the world's median heat flow, 200 °C rock sits about 8.5 km down.

Gradients by region are quoted from the US Geological Survey and the Geological Society. The depth table and maps are a Zemanium conduction model (labelled [MODEL]) run on the measured values of the IHFC Global Heat Flow Database 2024.

01 / Answer

## What is the geothermal gradient?

It is the increase in temperature per unit of depth below the surface, usually given in °C per kilometre. Away from plate boundaries and hotspots, temperature rises about 25 to 30 °C per kilometre in the lithosphere, by the Geological Society's teaching guidance.

| Where | Gradient | Source |
|---|---|---|
| Typical continental crust | 25 to 30 °C per km | Geological Society |
| Most of the contiguous United States, to 2 km | 15 to 35 °C per km | USGS, Nathenson and Guffanti |
| Eastern United States, average | 25 °C per km | USGS, Nathenson and Guffanti |
| Western United States, average | 34 °C per km | USGS, Nathenson and Guffanti |
| World median heat flow (59 mW/m²), at the surface | about 24 °C per km | Zemanium [MODEL] on IHFC data |
| Region around Milford, Utah (92 mW/m²) | about 37 °C per km | Zemanium [MODEL] on IHFC data |
| Region around Tirana, Albania (31 mW/m²) | about 12 °C per km | Zemanium [MODEL] on IHFC data |

02 / Formula

## How the geothermal gradient is calculated.

Heat flows up through rock by conduction. The gradient is the heat flow divided by the rock's thermal conductivity:

`gradient (°C per km) = heat flow (mW/m²) / thermal conductivity (W/m/K)`

At the world's median continental heat flow of 59 milliwatts per square metre and a conductivity of 2.5 W/m/K, the gradient at the surface is 59 / 2.5 = 23.6 °C per kilometre. The USGS derived an average conductivity of 2.5 ± 0.8 W/m/°C for US rock between a few hundred metres and 2 km. Rock that conducts heat poorly, such as thick sediment, steepens the gradient; rock that conducts well, such as granite, flattens it.

The gradient also eases with depth, because part of the surface heat flow is made inside the crust by radioactive decay. Our model takes 1 µW/m³ of that heat in the top 10 km and a surface temperature of 12 °C.

03 / Depth

## How deep do you have to drill to reach a given temperature?

We ran the conduction model on every measured onshore cell of the IHFC Global Heat Flow Database 2024: 51,882 values in 4,515 cells of one degree. The table gives the share of measured continental area where each temperature lies within each depth, and the median depth.

| Temperature | within 5 km | 7 km | 10 km | 12 km | 15 km | median depth |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 150 °C | 30% | 63% | 86% | 92% | 97% | 6.1 km |
| 200 °C | 9% | 32% | 65% | 78% | 89% | 8.5 km |
| 250 °C | 3% | 13% | 42% | 58% | 75% | 10.9 km |
| 400 °C | 0.3% | 1.5% | 7.5% | 14% | 30% | 18.5 km |

[MODEL] on measured data · 27 November 2026

![Line chart of the share of measured continental area where 150, 200, 250 and 400 °C lie within drilling depths from 3 to 15 km, with uncertainty bands for rock conductivity](https://zemanium.com/assets/charts/depth-to-temperature-reach.webp)

Bands show rock conductivity from 2.2 to 3.0 W/m/K. The dotted lines mark Fervo's 5.9 km well drilled in 21 days in 2026 and the deepest hole ever drilled, Kola, at 12.26 km. Free to reuse under CC BY 4.0 with credit to Zemanium.

For 200 °C the median depth ranges from 7.4 to 10.3 km across that conductivity band. Unmeasured land is left out, not counted as cold.

04 / Map

## Where the heat is closest to the surface.

![World map of the modelled depth to 200 °C in every measured one-degree cell of continental land; shallow cells in orange cluster in the western United States, central Europe, East Africa and around the Pacific](https://zemanium.com/assets/charts/depth-to-200c-map.webp)

Depth to 200 °C from the median heat flow in each measured one-degree cell, IHFC Global Heat Flow Database 2024. Blank land is unmeasured. [MODEL] on measured data; free to reuse under CC BY 4.0 with credit to Zemanium.

The shallowest heat follows young tectonics and volcanism: the western United States, Iceland, East Africa's rift, Indonesia, New Zealand and the rim of the Pacific, where the EIA notes most major geothermal resources sit. Old continental interiors run cooler. Local hot spots can be far hotter than their region: Cape Station in Utah drills into a local anomaly inside a region whose median heat flow puts 200 °C at 5.3 km. Close-up maps of the United States and Europe, with the depth to 200 °C in every measured US state, are on our [geothermal map](https://zemanium.com/guides/geothermal-map).

05 / Variation

## Why the gradient changes from place to place.

- Heat flow from below. Thin, young or stretched crust, rifts and volcanic arcs let more heat through.
- Rock conductivity. The USGS found gradients raised where thick, poorly conducting sediments lie, such as the Atlantic Coastal Plain and basins of the Great Plains.
- Moving water. Hot water rising along faults carries heat upward, which is what makes a conventional hydrothermal field.
- Heat made in the rock. Granite rich in uranium, thorium and potassium adds heat of its own.

06 / Power

## What the gradient means for geothermal power.

A binary power plant can run on water from about 110 °C, and flash plants on 200 °C and hotter, by the national laboratories' cost baseline. On a typical gradient that means drilling several kilometres; on a steep one, far less. Iceland's IDDP-2 well logged 426 °C at about 4.55 km.

Hotter rock yields more electricity per well, so the gradient sets how many wells a plant needs. Enhanced geothermal and superhot rock projects drill deeper to reach that heat in more places. Our guides to [geothermal wells](https://zemanium.com/guides/geothermal-wells), [enhanced geothermal systems](https://zemanium.com/guides/enhanced-geothermal-systems) and [superhot rock](https://zemanium.com/guides/superhot-rock-geothermal) pick up from here, and the [cost guide](https://zemanium.com/guides/geothermal-electricity-cost) shows what depth does to the price.

07 / Questions

## Common questions.

### What is the average geothermal gradient?

About 25 to 30 °C per kilometre in continental crust away from plate boundaries. On the world's median measured heat flow of 59 mW/m² and typical rock, it is about 24 °C per kilometre at the surface.

### How do you calculate the geothermal gradient?

Divide the heat flow by the rock's thermal conductivity. At 59 mW/m² and 2.5 W/m/K, the gradient is 23.6 °C per kilometre. In a borehole, divide the temperature difference between two depths by the distance between them.

### How hot is it 1 km underground?

On a typical gradient of 25 to 30 °C per kilometre and a surface temperature near 12 °C, rock 1 km down is about 37 to 42 °C. In the western United States, with an average gradient of 34 °C per kilometre, it is closer to 46 °C.

### How deep do you need to drill to reach 200 °C?

About 8.5 km at the median of the world's measured continental heat flow, and less than 5 km in 9% of measured land, by our model on the IHFC database. Geothermal regions such as parts of Utah and Nevada reach it far shallower.

### Where is the geothermal gradient highest?

Near plate boundaries, rifts and volcanoes: Iceland, the western United States, East Africa, Indonesia, the Philippines, New Zealand and the Pacific rim. Old continental shields have the lowest gradients.

3. Geological Society of London, [Geothermal gradient and magma generation, teachers' guidance](https://www.geolsoc.org.uk/media/uitj2igl/ks5-geothermal-gradient-teachers-notes.pdf), read 27 November 2026.

# Geothermal map: where the Earth's heat is closest to the surface.

These maps show where geothermal heat lies shallowest, from 51,882 heat-flow measurements on land in the IHFC Global Heat Flow Database 2024. The world map shows measured heat flow. The maps of the United States and Europe turn it into the depth at which rock reaches 200 °C, where flash power plants start, with our conduction model. Nevada has the shallowest heat of any US state: 200 °C at about 4.4 km at its median heat flow. In Europe, Iceland leads at 3.6 km.

Heat flow is measured, compiled by the International Heat Flow Commission. Depths are Zemanium model results on that data, labelled [MODEL]. Outlines are from Natural Earth. Every map is free to reuse under CC BY 4.0 with credit to Zemanium.

01 / World

## World geothermal map: measured heat flow.

![World geothermal map of measured heat flow on land, median per one-degree cell; the highest values in orange run along the western United States, Iceland, the East African Rift, Indonesia, Japan and New Zealand, and old continental interiors in grey run lowest](https://zemanium.com/assets/charts/geothermal-heat-flow-map.webp)

Median heat flow in every one-degree cell of land with a measurement, IHFC Global Heat Flow Database 2024. Squares mark the 166 cells holding a value above 250 mW/m². Blank land is unmeasured. Measured; free to reuse under CC BY 4.0 with credit to Zemanium.

Heat flow is the heat escaping through each square metre of ground, in milliwatts per square metre (mW/m²): the temperature gradient measured in a borehole times the conductivity of the rock. The median of the world's measured continental cells is 59 mW/m², which puts 200 °C at about 8.5 km by our model. The hottest belts follow plate boundaries, rifts and young volcanoes: the western United States, Iceland, the East African Rift, Indonesia, Japan, New Zealand and the rim of the Pacific, where the EIA notes most major geothermal resources sit. The squares mark convective hot spots, where hot water rising through the rock carries heat faster than conduction alone.

![World map of the modelled depth to 200 °C in every measured one-degree cell of continental land; shallow cells in orange cluster in the western United States, central Europe, East Africa and around the Pacific](https://zemanium.com/assets/charts/depth-to-200c-map.webp)

Depth to 200 °C from the median heat flow in each measured one-degree cell. [MODEL] on measured data; free to reuse under CC BY 4.0 with credit to Zemanium.

02 / United States

## Geothermal map of the United States.

![Geothermal map of the contiguous United States showing the modelled depth to 200 °C in every measured half-degree cell; the shallowest heat in dark orange covers Nevada, Idaho, Oregon, California and Utah, with The Geysers, Salton Sea, Coso, Cape Station and McGinness Hills marked](https://zemanium.com/assets/charts/geothermal-map-united-states.webp)

Depth to 200 °C from the median heat flow in each measured half-degree cell. Squares mark cells with a value above 250 mW/m², convective hot spots the conduction model leaves out. Dots mark operating or pilot fields at approximate locations. [MODEL] on measured data; free to reuse under CC BY 4.0 with credit to Zemanium.

The shallow heat of the United States covers the Great Basin of Nevada and western Utah, the Snake River Plain of Idaho, Oregon and California. That is where the country's geothermal power plants are: most are in western states and Hawaii, and California leads in geothermal electricity, according to the EIA. Nevada publishes the output of every plant; our [power plant guide](https://zemanium.com/guides/geothermal-power-plants) lists all of them.

Squares mark 155 half-degree cells with a value above 250 mW/m² in the map's frame, all but one west of the 104th meridian. The Atlantic coast and Great Lakes states in the table, measured in fewer places, run cooler: 200 °C lies 9.1 km down or deeper at their medians.

04 / Europe

## Geothermal map of Europe.

![Geothermal map of Europe showing the modelled depth to 200 °C in every measured half-degree cell; the shallowest heat in dark orange covers Iceland, France, Germany, Tuscany, Hungary and western Turkey, while Finland and Ukraine in grey run deepest, with Larderello, Hellisheiði, Kızıldere, Geretsried and Soultz-sous-Forêts marked](https://zemanium.com/assets/charts/geothermal-map-europe.webp)

Depth to 200 °C from the median heat flow in each measured half-degree cell. Squares mark the 11 cells with a value above 250 mW/m². Dots mark operating or pilot fields at approximate locations. [MODEL] on measured data; free to reuse under CC BY 4.0 with credit to Zemanium.

Europe's shallowest heat lies in Iceland, Tuscany, the Upper Rhine Graben between France and Germany, the Paris and Molasse basins, Hungary's Pannonian Basin and western Turkey. Tuscany's Larderello field ran the first geothermal power plant, in 1904. The old shields of Finland, Scandinavia and Ukraine run coldest, with 200 °C at 11.7 km or deeper.

| Region | Heat-flow values | Median heat flow (mW/m²) | Depth to 150 °C (km) | Depth to 200 °C (km) |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Iceland | 117 | 133 | 2.6 | 3.6 |
| Upper Rhine Graben, France and Germany | 266 | 106 | 3.3 | 4.5 |
| Tuscany, Italy | 98 | 104.7 | 3.3 | 4.6 |
| Paris Basin, France | 216 | 92 | 3.8 | 5.3 |
| Molasse Basin, Bavaria | 92 | 86.6 | 4.1 | 5.6 |
| Pannonian Basin, Hungary | 260 | 84.1 | 4.2 | 5.8 |
| Western Turkey | 199 | 80 | 4.4 | 6.1 |
| Iberia | 923 | 74 | 4.8 | 6.7 |
| North German Basin | 459 | 70 | 5.1 | 7.1 |
| Great Britain | 267 | 64.8 | 5.6 | 7.7 |
| Ukrainian Shield | 535 | 46 | 8.2 | 11.7 |
| Finland and northern Scandinavia | 200 | 38 | 10.5 | 15.0 |

[MODEL] · regions drawn as latitude and longitude boxes · 28 November 2026

Eavor's closed-loop plant at Geretsried sits in the Molasse Basin; how it works is in our [closed-loop geothermal guide](https://zemanium.com/guides/closed-loop-geothermal).

05 / Method

## How to read these maps.

- Heat flow is measured. Each cell shows the median of the values inside it: one-degree cells on the world map, half-degree cells on the regional maps.
- Depth is modelled. We solve heat conduction down from the surface with rock conductivity of 2.5 W/m/K, 1 µW/m³ of heat produced in the top 10 km and a surface at 12 °C. A conductivity of 2.2 to 3.0 W/m/K moves the world median depth to 200 °C between 7.4 and 10.3 km, as our [geothermal gradient guide](https://zemanium.com/guides/geothermal-gradient) shows.
- Values above 250 mW/m², 2,023 of them, mark places where moving water carries the heat. Conduction does not describe them, so they are drawn as squares and left out of the depths.
- Blank land is unmeasured, not cold.

The world map of depth to 150, 200, 250 and 400 °C, and the share of land within reach of each drilling depth, are in the gradient guide. What the heat is worth in a power plant is in our [power plant guide](https://zemanium.com/guides/geothermal-power-plants).

06 / Questions

## Common questions.

### Where is geothermal energy found in the United States?

Mostly in the West. Nevada, Idaho, California, Oregon, Colorado, Utah and Arizona reach 200 °C within about 6.2 km at their median heat flow, by our model, and most US geothermal power plants are in western states and Hawaii, according to the EIA.

### Which US state has the most geothermal energy?

Nevada has the shallowest heat, with 200 °C at about 4.4 km at its median heat flow of 109 mW/m². California generates the most geothermal electricity, according to the EIA, led by The Geysers.

### Where is geothermal energy found in Europe?

In Iceland, Tuscany, the Upper Rhine Graben, the Paris and Molasse basins, Hungary's Pannonian Basin and western Turkey, where 200 °C lies between 3.6 and 6.1 km at the regional median, by our model.

### What does a geothermal map show?

Usually heat flow, the heat escaping through the ground in mW/m², or the temperature at a given depth. Our maps show measured heat flow worldwide and the modelled depth to 200 °C in the United States and Europe.

### How deep do you have to drill for geothermal energy?

For electricity, to rock of about 110 °C or hotter for a binary plant and about 200 °C for a flash plant, by NLR's baseline. At the state median, 150 °C lies at 3.2 km in Nevada and 7.3 km in Texas, and much shallower at local hot spots, by our model.

2. Natural Earth, [1:50m countries and 1:110m states](https://www.naturalearthdata.com/), public domain.

# Geothermal power plants: how they work, the three types, and what they produce.

A geothermal power plant brings hot water or steam up through wells, uses it to spin a turbine, and sends the cooled water back underground. There are three types: dry steam plants use steam straight from the ground, flash plants boil high-pressure hot water into steam, and binary plants pass the heat to a second fluid that boils at a lower temperature. The world had 17,173 MW of geothermal power capacity at the end of 2025, and the US fleet ran at a 65.9% capacity factor.

Plant types and figures are quoted from the EIA, the National Laboratory of the Rockies (NLR, formerly NREL), ThinkGeoEnergy and Calpine. Nevada plant output is measured and operator-reported to the Nevada Division of Minerals. Work-per-kilogram figures are Zemanium model results, labelled [MODEL].

01 / Mechanism

## How does a geothermal power plant work?

![Diagram of how a geothermal power plant works: a production well brings hot water and steam from the reservoir, a separator splits off the steam, the steam spins a turbine and generator, a condenser and cooling tower turn it back into water, and an injection well returns the water to the reservoir](https://zemanium.com/assets/charts/geothermal-power-plant-diagram.svg)

A flash geothermal power plant, the most common type. Binary plants swap the separator for a heat exchanger and a second working fluid. Not to scale. Free to reuse under CC BY 4.0 with credit to Zemanium.

1. Production wells reach a reservoir of hot water or steam, or hot rock that engineers have made permeable. The EIA notes that plants use water or steam at 300 to 700 °F and that some wells go as deep as about 2 miles.
2. The fluid rises to the surface under its own pressure or with a downhole pump.
3. Its heat drives a turbine: as steam directly, as steam flashed from hot water, or through a heat exchanger that boils a second fluid.
4. The turbine turns a generator, which feeds the grid.
5. The cooled water goes back down injection wells, keeping reservoir pressure up and returning the fluid to be heated again.

Nothing burns, and the heat does not depend on weather, so a geothermal plant runs day and night. In 2025 the US fleet produced 65.9% of what its available capacity could deliver running flat out, against 24.0% for solar and 33.8% for wind, by the EIA's count.

### How is geothermal energy produced?

Geothermal energy comes from deep inside the Earth, produced by the slow breakdown of radioactive particles, a process that happens naturally in all rocks, by the EIA's account. The heat flows up through the crust, so the deeper you go, the hotter the rock. Where it meets water in permeable rock it forms a reservoir of hot water or steam, and a power plant turns that into electricity in the steps above. How fast rock heats with depth is in our [geothermal gradient guide](https://zemanium.com/guides/geothermal-gradient), and where the heat lies shallowest is on our [geothermal map](https://zemanium.com/guides/geothermal-map).

02 / Types

## What are the three types of geothermal power plants?

| Type | How it works | Resource | Example |
|---|---|---|---|
| Dry steam | Steam from the reservoir goes straight to the turbine | rare steam-dominated fields | The Geysers, California, producing since 1960; the first geothermal power plant, Italy, 1904 |
| Flash steam | High-pressure hot water drops in pressure at the surface and part of it flashes to steam; the most common type, by the EIA's account | about 200 °C and hotter (NLR baseline) | NLR's representative flash plant: 225 °C water at 2.5 km, 40 MW |
| Binary cycle | Geothermal water heats a second working fluid with a lower boiling point, which drives the turbine in an organic Rankine cycle; the geothermal water never touches the turbine and goes back underground, with no air emissions | about 110 to 200 °C in NLR's baseline; commercial cycles run up to 300 °C | NLR's representative binary plant: 175 °C water at 1.5 km, 30 MW |

Some sites combine flash and binary units. Flash plants produce more power per well because they run hotter, so they need fewer wells for the same output and generally cost less per kilowatt, by NLR's analysis. Binary plants open up the much larger supply of moderate-temperature water.

### What is an organic Rankine cycle?

It is the cycle inside a binary plant. A Rankine cycle boils a fluid, expands the vapour through a turbine, condenses it and pumps it back. Binary plants use a working fluid with a boiling point below that of water, so 110 to 200 °C water can boil it.

03 / Temperature

## Why hotter water makes cheaper power.

The useful work a kilogram of geothermal fluid can deliver rises steeply with its temperature. Our physics model gives the flow exergy, the maximum work available at the wellhead:

| Reservoir temperature | Maximum work per kilogram |
|---|---|
| 200 °C | 172 kJ/kg |
| 300 °C | 354 kJ/kg |
| 400 °C | 566 to 617 kJ/kg |
| 450 °C | 681 to 756 kJ/kg |

[MODEL] · IAPWS water properties · 27 November 2026

Moving from 200 °C to 400 °C more than triples the work per kilogram, so each well powers more of the plant. That is the case for [superhot rock geothermal](https://zemanium.com/guides/superhot-rock-geothermal). How deep that heat lies is in our [geothermal gradient guide](https://zemanium.com/guides/geothermal-gradient), and what the wells cost is in the [wells guide](https://zemanium.com/guides/geothermal-wells).

04 / New plants

## Enhanced and closed-loop geothermal plants.

- Enhanced geothermal systems make a reservoir in hot rock that lacks water or cracks, by opening fractures and circulating water between wells. Fervo Energy's Cape Station in Utah sent first power on 24 September 2026. More in our [enhanced geothermal guide](https://zemanium.com/guides/enhanced-geothermal-systems).
- Closed-loop systems circulate a fluid through sealed wells and take heat by conduction, with no fracturing. Eavor's plant at Geretsried, Germany, has sent power to the grid since December 2025, and its loop circulates by thermosiphon without a pump after start-up, by the company's account. More in our [closed-loop geothermal guide](https://zemanium.com/guides/closed-loop-geothermal).

Both still run a flash or binary plant on the surface. The companies building them are in our [guide to geothermal companies](https://zemanium.com/guides/geothermal-companies).

07 / Questions

## Common questions.

### How does a geothermal power plant generate electricity?

Wells bring hot water or steam from underground. Its heat spins a turbine, directly as steam, as steam flashed from hot water, or through a second fluid in a binary plant. The turbine drives a generator, and the cooled water is injected back underground.

### What are the three types of geothermal power plants?

Dry steam, flash steam and binary cycle. Dry steam plants use steam from the reservoir, flash plants turn high-pressure hot water into steam, and binary plants heat a second fluid with a lower boiling point. Flash plants are the most common, according to the EIA.

### What is a binary cycle power plant?

A geothermal plant that passes the heat of the underground water to a second working fluid, which boils and drives the turbine in an organic Rankine cycle. The geothermal water stays in a closed loop and returns underground. Binary plants suit water of about 110 to 200 °C.

### How much electricity does a geothermal power plant produce?

Plants range from a few megawatts to hundreds. NLR's representative plants are 30 to 50 MW. In Nevada in 2025 the largest single plant code, McGinness Hills 3, produced 562 GWh, and the state's 27 reporting plants produced 5,031 GWh.

### Where is the largest geothermal power plant?

The Geysers in northern California, a complex of 13 plants operated by Calpine with about 725 MW of capacity, is the largest geothermal power complex in the world by Calpine's account.

### Which country produces the most geothermal power?

The United States, with 3,953 MW installed at the end of 2025, followed by Indonesia with 2,742 MW and the Philippines with 2,034 MW, according to ThinkGeoEnergy.

### How efficient is a geothermal power plant?

Geothermal plants convert about 12% of the heat they draw from the ground into electricity on average worldwide, and the best reported, at Darajat in Indonesia, about 21%, by the 2014 worldwide review of Zarrouk and Moon. The heat itself costs nothing, so the efficiency sets how many wells a plant needs.

### Are geothermal power plants bad for the environment?

Their footprint is small. Over their life they emit a median 37 g of CO2-equivalent per kWh, against 486 for natural gas, by NLR's 2021 review, and they scrub hydrogen sulfide and reinject their water. Our guide to the [environmental impacts of geothermal energy](https://zemanium.com/guides/geothermal-environmental-impacts) has the full data.

# Geothermal stocks in 2026: the listed producers and what their plants deliver.

The two US-listed companies that run mainly on geothermal power are Ormat Technologies (NYSE: ORA), the largest, and Fervo Energy (Nasdaq: FRVO), listed in May 2026. Six more listed companies in Indonesia, Kenya, New Zealand and Canada own large geothermal fleets. Below is each one, its capacity from its own reports, and the public plant record behind the numbers.

Capacity figures are company statements. Nevada output figures are measured and operator-reported to the state regulator. Independent analysis from public records; not investment advice. Zemanium holds no position in any security.

01 / Companies

## Which geothermal companies are publicly traded?

Eight listed companies own large geothermal fleets. The table gives each one's exchange, ticker and capacity as the company reports it.

| **Fervo Energy** | Nasdaq: FRVO | Enhanced geothermal developer; listed May 2026; Cape Station, Utah, first power 24 Sep 2026 from a first unit of about 33 MW; 900 MW contracted | company, 24 Sep 2026 [[3]](https://zemanium.com/guides/geothermal-stocks#s3) |
| **Pertamina Geothermal Energy** | IDX: PGEO | 1,932 MW installed in Indonesia, of which 727 MW operated on its own and 1,205 MW with partners | company, Q2 2025 [[4]](https://zemanium.com/guides/geothermal-stocks#s4) |
| **Barito Renewables (Star Energy Geothermal)** | IDX: BREN | 935.55 MW at Salak, Darajat and Wayang Windu, Indonesia | company, 2026 [[5]](https://zemanium.com/guides/geothermal-stocks#s5) |

02 / Fervo

## Fervo Energy (FRVO): what the public record shows.

Fervo priced its initial public offering at $27 a share on 12 May 2026 and sold 70 million shares; trading on Nasdaq began on 13 May. Its first commercial plant, Cape Station in Utah, reached first power on 24 September 2026, with a first phase of about 100 MW planned, by the company's account.

Fervo's pilot well pair, Project Red in Nevada, is the only enhanced geothermal system with a public monthly production record. Its wellhead temperature read 347 °F at its 2024 plateau and 316 °F in July 2026. We track it every month against a forecast registered on 19 November 2026.

[Open the Project Red tracker ](https://zemanium.com/fervo-project-red)

Nevada publishes monthly output for every geothermal plant in the state. Statewide output was 5,044 GWh in 2019, peaked at 5,391 GWh in 2023 and was 5,031 GWh in 2025. The McGinness Hills complex, whose operator of record is Ormat Nevada and its ORNI subsidiaries, is the largest single site in the record.

04 / Method

## How to read a geothermal producer.

- **Capacity factor.** Energy produced in a year divided by capacity times 8,760 hours. Geothermal plants run day and night, so a falling figure usually means the wells deliver less heat.
- **Reservoir temperature trend.** A well that cools needs makeup drilling to hold output. The regulator records in Nevada show it field by field.
- **Cost per megawatt-hour.** Our [cost guide](https://zemanium.com/guides/geothermal-electricity-cost) shows which inputs move it, and the [power-cost model](https://zemanium.com/confidence/) prices a plant under your assumptions.

05 / Questions

## Common questions.

### Is Fervo Energy publicly traded?

Yes. Fervo Energy trades on Nasdaq under the ticker FRVO. It priced its initial public offering at $27 a share on 12 May 2026 and began trading on 13 May 2026.

### What is the largest geothermal stock?

By capacity, Pertamina Geothermal Energy (IDX: PGEO) reports 1,932 MW installed including partner-operated plants. Among US-listed companies, Ormat Technologies (NYSE: ORA) is the largest, with a 1,853 MW portfolio that also includes solar and storage.

### Are there geothermal stocks outside the United States?

Yes. Pertamina Geothermal Energy and Barito Renewables trade in Jakarta, KenGen in Nairobi, Mercury NZ and Contact Energy in New Zealand, and Polaris Renewable Energy in Toronto.

### Where can I check a geothermal plant's actual output?

In Nevada, the Division of Minerals publishes monthly output for every plant and monthly temperature for every well. Our Nevada plant file and the Project Red tracker take their numbers from that record. Across the United States, the EIA publishes monthly generation by plant.

5. Barito Renewables, [Darajat Unit 3 retrofit, installed capacity 935.55 MW](https://baritorenewables.co.id/en/press-release/barito-renewables-completes-star-energy-darajat-unit-3-retrofit-bringing-installed-capacity-to-93555-mw).
6. KenGen, [results for the year to June 2025](https://kengen.co.ke/kengen-posts-10-5b-profits-in-2025-up-54-on-growth-and-efficiency-gains).
7. Mercury NZ, [geothermal strategy](https://mercury.co.nz/investors/news/2025-july---geothermal-strategy), July 2025.
8. Contact Energy, [Te Huka Unit 3 agreement with Microsoft](https://contact.co.nz/investor-centre/news/2023/contact-signs-ten-year-renewable-energy-agreement-with-microsoft), May 2023; NZ Herald, [Contact Energy flicks the switch on Te Huka 3](https://nzherald.co.nz/business/contact-energy-flicks-the-switch-on-te-huka-3/ESBRCP7XMJFNZLGO4JSPTMS3LA), October 2024.
9. Polaris Renewable Energy, [second quarter 2026 results](https://nasdaq.com/press-release/polaris-renewable-energy-announces-q2-2026-results-2026-07-30), 30 July 2026.

Guide · [Toni Zemani](https://zemanium.com/about#toni-zemani) · 27 November 2026

# Geothermal wells: how deep they go, what they cost and how long they last.

Geothermal power wells reach 1.5 to 2.5 kilometres for a typical conventional plant and 3 to 7 kilometres for deep enhanced geothermal, by the national laboratories' cost baseline. Drilling one costs millions of dollars: Fervo Energy's Cape Station wells fell from $9.4 million to $4.8 million each. They produce for decades, while the water they bring up slowly cools; in Nevada's public record the median field ran about 1.9 °F cooler each year.

Drilling figures come from the National Laboratory of the Rockies (NLR, formerly NREL) and company statements, labelled as such. Field temperatures are measured and operator-reported to the Nevada Division of Minerals; yearly rates are computed by Zemanium from that record.

01 / In brief

## Geothermal wells at a glance.

- Depth: NLR's representative conventional plants draw on 175 °C water at 1.5 km and 225 °C water at 2.5 km; deep enhanced geothermal targets 3 to 7 km. The EIA notes some geothermal wells reach about 2 miles.
- Cost: drilling makes up 30% to 57% of a new plant's capital cost. Fervo's Cape Station wells cost $346 to $634 per foot drilled, against $995 and $1,107 at its Project Red pilot.
- Speed: the fastest of the first six Cape Station wells took 20 days for 13,289 feet. Fervo reported 19,448 feet in 21 days at its Sawtooth 7 well in 2026.
- Life: NLR's cost baseline assumes 30 years for plant and reservoir. The Geysers in California has produced power since 1960.
- Cooling: in 11 of 18 long-running Nevada fields the produced water is more than 5 °F cooler than in its first recorded year.

02 / Depth

## How deep are geothermal wells?

As deep as the heat requires. Geothermal power plants need water or steam at 300 to 700 °F, according to the EIA, and how far down that sits depends on the local geology. Recent wells with public records:

| Well | Measured depth | Temperature | Drilling time | Basis |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| GDC-36, The Geysers, California (2023) | 9,000 ft (2,743 m) | steam above 475 °F (246 °C) | 69 days | NLR 2025 |
| Project Red pair, Nevada | 11,211 and 11,220 ft (3.42 km) | 376 °F (191 °C) maximum | 59 and 72 days | NLR 2025 |
| Utah FORGE 16B(78)-32 (2023) | 10,947 ft (3.34 km) | research site | 75 days | NLR 2025 |
| Cape Station, Utah, 14 horizontal wells (2023 to 2024) | 13,272 to 15,347 ft (4.0 to 4.7 km), laterals about 4,700 ft | 444 °F (229 °C) maximum | 20 to 34 days for the first six | NLR 2025 |
| Sawtooth 7, Utah (2026) | 19,448 ft (5.9 km) with a 7,500 ft lateral | about 238 °C rock | 21 days | company statement |
| IDDP-2, Reykjanes, Iceland | logged at about 4,550 m | 426 °C | research well | World Geothermal Congress paper |

Measured depth is the length of the hole. Horizontal wells such as Cape Station's run sideways for thousands of feet at their target, so their vertical depth is shorter than their measured depth.

03 / Cost

## How much does it cost to drill a geothermal well?

Millions of dollars per well, and falling. NLR's 2025 analysis of Fervo's wells, using data Fervo supplied:

| Well | Total depth | Days | Feet per day | Cost per foot |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Project Red 1 | 11,220 ft | 71 | 158 | $994.62 |
| Project Red 2 | 11,211 ft | 58 | 193 | $1,106.74 |
| Cape Station 3 | 13,316 ft | 33.75 | 312 | $633.45 |
| Cape Station 4 | 13,272 ft | 25.91 | 440 | $471.59 |
| Cape Station 5 | 13,601 ft | 24.26 | 504 | $395.71 |
| Cape Station 6 | 13,289 ft | 20.1 | 567 | $346.45 |
| Cape Station 7 | 13,949 ft | 23.71 | 472 | $394.08 |
| Cape Station 8 | 13,734 ft | 22.27 | 539 | $357.36 |

At $346.45 a foot, Cape Station 6 cost about $4.6 million to drill, before completion. Fervo itself reported its Cape Station well cost falling from $9.4 million to $4.8 million. NLR attributes the gains to diamond (PDC) bits, drilling practices that remove the limits on speed one by one, and drilling several wells from one pad, and its 2025 cost curves sit 12% to 24% below the 2017 baseline for vertical wells and 18% to 26% below for horizontal ones.

Casing and cementing alone make up 30% to 40% or more of a well's cost, according to the US Department of Energy. And not every well finds what it is drilled for: NLR's baseline assumes 60% of exploration wells at a new conventional site succeed.

What well costs do to the price of power is in our [cost guide](https://zemanium.com/guides/geothermal-electricity-cost), and the [LCOE calculator](https://zemanium.com/lcoe-calculator) turns any capital cost into dollars per megawatt-hour.

04 / Lifespan

## How long do geothermal wells last?

Decades. NLR's cost baseline assumes a 30-year life for plant and reservoir, and The Geysers in California has produced electricity since 1960, according to the EIA. Over that time the water a field produces cools as injected water draws heat from the rock, and operators drill makeup wells to hold output.

Nevada publishes the monthly temperature of every producing geothermal well. We tracked 18 fields with ten or more years of record; ten of them, from fastest cooling to warming, show the spread:

| Field (regulator code) | Years | First-year mean | 2025 mean | Change per year |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Blue Mountain (BLU) | 2009 to 2025 | 368 °F | 281 °F | -5.4 °F |
| WRS2 (WRS2) | 2015 to 2025 | 261 °F | 212 °F | -4.9 °F |
| Jersey Valley (JVP) | 2012 to 2025 | 331 °F | 292 °F | -2.9 °F |
| McGinness Hills 2 (MGH2) | 2015 to 2025 | 336 °F | 307 °F | -2.9 °F |
| Brady Hot Springs (BHS) | 2012 to 2025 | 280 °F | 248 °F | -2.5 °F |
| McGinness Hills (MGH) | 2012 to 2025 | 335 °F | 306 °F | -2.2 °F |
| Steamboat (STB) | 2012 to 2025 | 290 °F | 263 °F | -2.1 °F |
| Patua (PTA) | 2013 to 2025 | 303 °F | 293 °F | -0.8 °F |
| Dixie Valley (DXV) | 2012 to 2025 | 330 °F | 330 °F | 0.0 °F |
| Stillwater (STW) | 2009 to 2025 | 270 °F | 297 °F | +1.7 °F |

The median of all 18 fields is a change of about -1.9 °F per year. A field's mean also moves when operators add or retire wells, so these figures describe the produced water, not the rock alone. All 18 fields are in our guide [is geothermal energy renewable](https://zemanium.com/guides/is-geothermal-energy-renewable), and every yearly value is in [one JSON file](https://zemanium.com/data/nevada-field-temperature.json), CC BY 4.0.

The clearest single well-pair record is Fervo's Project Red, which went from 347 °F at its 2024 plateau to 316 °F in July 2026. Our [Project Red tracker](https://zemanium.com/fervo-project-red) scores a forecast of it, registered on 19 November 2026, against the regulator's record every month.

05 / Integrity

## What fails first in a geothermal well.

The steel and cement. A well heats when it produces and cools when cold water is pumped in or the well is shut in, and each cycle stresses the casing and its couplings. A 2018 review of 20 high-temperature wells found that most well failures came from thermal stress during quenching or the start of production. Iceland's IDDP-2 had its production casing damaged between 2,307 and 2,380 m, presumably by repeated heating and cooling. Downhole electronics stop working near 210 to 225 °C.

That is our field. We rebuilt IDDP-1's production casing in a model and ran it through the well's recorded history, and we are building Pandora, a casing joint for wells at 450 to 500 °C. The [superhot rock guide](https://zemanium.com/guides/superhot-rock-geothermal) has the record and the sources.

06 / Heat pumps

## Geothermal heat pump wells are a different thing.

A home or office geothermal heat pump uses the steady temperature a few hundred feet down; it makes no electricity. For a vertical system, holes about 4 inches across are drilled about 20 feet apart and 100 to 400 feet deep, according to the US Department of Energy. The shallowest power well in the table above goes more than 20 times deeper. The loops that go into those holes are explained in our guide to [closed-loop geothermal](https://zemanium.com/guides/closed-loop-geothermal).

07 / Questions

## Common questions.

### What is a geothermal well?

A hole drilled to bring the Earth's heat to the surface. Power plants use production wells that lift hot water or steam and injection wells that return it, typically 1.5 to 7 km deep. Geothermal heat pumps use boreholes 100 to 400 feet deep that hold a sealed loop of pipe.

### How deep is a geothermal well?

For power plants, typically 1.5 to 2.5 km for conventional hydrothermal sites and 3 to 7 km for deep enhanced geothermal, by the NLR baseline. Recent wells range from 9,000 feet at The Geysers to 19,448 feet of measured depth at Fervo's Sawtooth 7 in Utah. Heat pump boreholes are 100 to 400 feet.

### How much does a geothermal well cost?

Fervo Energy reported its Cape Station wells falling from $9.4 million to $4.8 million each. NLR's analysis puts those wells at $346 to $634 per foot drilled, and drilling at 30% to 57% of a new geothermal plant's capital cost.

### How long does a geothermal well last?

Wells and plants run for decades; NLR's baseline assumes 30 years, and The Geysers has produced since 1960. The water they produce cools over time: the median long-running Nevada field ran about 1.9 °F cooler each year, and operators add makeup wells to hold output.

### How long does it take to drill a geothermal well?

Weeks. The fastest of Fervo's first six Cape Station wells took 20 days for 13,289 feet, down from 58 to 72 days for its Project Red pilot wells, and the company reported 19,448 feet in 21 days in 2026. The Geysers GDC-36 well took 69 days for 9,000 feet.

### How hot is the water in a geothermal well?

Power plants use water or steam at 300 to 700 °F, according to the EIA. Cape Station's production test ran at about 195 °C (383 °F), and research wells in Iceland have met fluid above 400 °C.

08 / Sources
